    ServiceCollectionFakeExtensions

    MMCA.Common.Testing · MMCA.Common.Testing.Support · MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing/Support/ServiceCollectionFakeExtensions.cs:9 · Level 0 · class (static)

    • What it is: test helpers that swap a host's registration for a fake inside a test factory's ConfigureTestServices (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing/Support/ServiceCollectionFakeExtensions.cs:5-9).
    • Depends on: Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection only (IServiceCollection, ServiceDescriptor, ServiceLifetime, :1). No first-party dependency.
    • Concept introduced, the stale-fake guard. A plain RemoveAll plus Add silently succeeds when the host no longer registers the service at all, so a fake can outlive the dependency it stood in for and the test keeps passing against nothing real. Every overload here first requires an unkeyed registration of the service and throws InvalidOperationException naming the stale fake when there is none (:87-89). The members are declared in a C# extension(IServiceCollection services) block (:11), the extension-member form recorded in ADR-106. [Rubric §14, Testability] covers keeping host-level test doubles honest.
    • Walkthrough
      • ReplaceWithFake<TService, TFake>() (:24-30): reuses the lifetime of the LAST unkeyed registration, the one DI would have resolved (:28), and swaps in TFake.
      • ReplaceWithFake<TService, TFake>(ServiceLifetime lifetime) (:44-50): the same, with the lifetime given by the caller; the existence check still runs (:48).
      • ReplaceWithFake<TService>(TService instance) (:64-71): null-guards the instance (:67) and registers it as a singleton (:70).
      • LastUnkeyedRegistration (:74-90): walks the collection keeping the last descriptor whose service type matches and which is not keyed (:81), or throws.
      • Swap (:92-105): removes every matching unkeyed descriptor walking backwards from the end (:94-101), then adds the fake (:103). Keyed registrations are neither removed nor counted.
    • Why it's built this way: failing on a missing registration turns a fake that has drifted from the host into a red test instead of a silently meaningless one, and leaving keyed registrations alone keeps the swap from disturbing a keyed sibling of the same service type.
    • Where it's used: covered by MMCA.Common's own ServiceCollectionFakeExtensionsTests (see the per-project test rollup). The brief's usage-site slice lists no consumer call site outside the defining file.

    TestPolling

    MMCA.Common.Testing · MMCA.Common.Testing.Support · MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing/Support/TestPolling.cs:9 · Level 0 · class (static)

    • What it is: a poll-with-timeout helper for asynchronous integration assertions. It repeatedly probes a value until a condition holds or a budget runs out, and hands back the last probed value either way.
    • Depends on: BCL only (Task, DateTime, TimeSpan). No first-party dependency and no assertion library, so the caller keeps ownership of the assertion.
    • Concept introduced, replacing the pre-assert sleep. Anything that travels the outbox to a broker and back, or any other eventually-consistent path, arrives at a time the test cannot know (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing/Support/TestPolling.cs:3-8). A fixed Task.Delay before the assertion is both slow and flaky: too short and the suite reds intermittently, too long and every green run pays the worst case. Polling returns as soon as the condition holds and bounds the wait. [Rubric §14, Testability] assesses whether the suite is deterministic; [Rubric §6, CQRS & Event-Driven] is why the problem exists at all, since the outbox (ADR-003) is asynchronous by design and offers no synchronous handle to await.
    • Walkthrough
      • PollUntilAsync<T>(Func<Task<T>> probe, Func<T, bool> isSatisfied, TimeSpan? timeout = null, TimeSpan? interval = null) (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing/Support/TestPolling.cs:22-41): null-guards both delegates (:28-29), computes a deadline from the 60-second default budget (:31) and a 500 ms default interval (:32), probes once before the loop (:33), then loops while the condition is unmet and the deadline has not passed (:34-38).
      • The return is the design decision worth noticing: it returns last unconditionally (:40) rather than throwing on timeout, so a timed-out poll still fails on the caller's real assertion message rather than on a bare timeout exception (the doc states exactly this at :11-14).
    • Why it's built this way: bounding the wait and returning the last value keeps two properties at once, a fast green path (the loop exits on the first satisfying probe) and a diagnosable red path (the failure message describes the domain expectation, not the plumbing).
    • Where it's used: the cross-service tiers of both apps route every eventual assertion through it and say so in their own docs (MMCA.Store/Tests/Integration/MMCA.Store.CrossService.IntegrationTests/Infrastructure/CrossServiceTestBase.cs:15 and the ADC equivalent at MMCA.ADC/Tests/Integration/MMCA.ADC.CrossService.IntegrationTests/Infrastructure/CrossServiceTestBase.cs), with call sites such as MMCA.Store/Tests/Integration/MMCA.Store.CrossService.IntegrationTests/CrossService/ProductVariantChangedRoundTripTests.cs:28,48,51. MMCA.Common covers the helper itself, including the null-argument guards (MMCA.Common/Tests/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Tests/Support/TestPollingTests.cs:15-64).

An edge is consumer->peer in Aspire resource names (:19-23). [Rubric §7, Microservices Readiness] covers whether extracted services can actually find each other in production; [Rubric §14, Testability] covers catching the drift before deploy.     CrossServiceFixtureBase

    MMCA.Common.Testing · MMCA.Common.Testing.Fixtures · MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing/Fixtures/CrossServiceFixtureBase.cs:47 · Level 1 · class (abstract)

    • What it is: the shared scaffolding for the cross-service real-broker integration tier. It boots several service hosts in ONE process against a real Testcontainers SQL Server and a real Testcontainers RabbitMQ, so the genuine outbox to broker to consumer round-trip (and any real cross-service gRPC read) is exercised end to end rather than faked (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing/Fixtures/CrossServiceFixtureBase.cs:17-25).
    • Depends on: CrossServiceDataSource (the per-source declaration), plus Microsoft.Data.SqlClient, Testcontainers.MsSql, Testcontainers.RabbitMq, and xUnit's IAsyncLifetime (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing/Fixtures/CrossServiceFixtureBase.cs:1-4,47).
    • Concept introduced, the multi-host in-process topology and its configuration channel. Where SqlServerIntegrationTestFixtureBase<TEntryPoint> boots one host with the cross-service edges faked and no broker, this base owns a whole topology. Two mechanisms are load-bearing, and both are documented on the class. First, process environment variables are the only override channel these hosts honor (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing/Fixtures/CrossServiceFixtureBase.cs:26-39): each host reads its connection string, MessageBus settings, and JWT settings from builder.Configuration at configure-time, before builder.Build(), which is before WebApplicationFactory.ConfigureAppConfiguration deltas apply, so in-memory config would arrive too late. Second, because the one genuinely per-host key is the SQL connection string, hosts must boot strictly sequentially, and that is safe precisely because a booted host has already snapshotted its connection (the data-source resolver, the context factory, the outbox processor, and the broker receiver are all built during StartAsync). A third paragraph of the class doc (:40-45) adds host isolation: every host factory calls CrossServiceHostIsolation.IsolateCrossServiceHost<TEntryPoint>() so a host does not adopt its peers' module assemblies (see HostScopedAssemblyProvider). [Rubric §7, Microservices Readiness] assesses whether extracted services really do collaborate over their declared transports; [Rubric §6, CQRS & Event-Driven] covers the outbox path (ADR-003); [Rubric §8, Data Architecture] covers database-per-service (ADR-006); and [Rubric §14, Testability] covers shipping the whole topology as a reusable base.
    • Walkthrough
      • State: the private DummyBearerAuthority constant (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing/Fixtures/CrossServiceFixtureBase.cs:51), the private CrossServiceApplicationNamespace constant "cross-service-tests" (:54), the original-environment snapshot map (:56), the two nullable containers (:58-59), and the public RabbitMqConnectionString (:62).
      • Subclass knobs: DataSources (:69, the logical sources in the order their databases are created), MigrationsAssemblyPrefix (:76, so each named source gets {prefix}.{LogicalName} exactly as production does), BootHostsAsync (:152) and DisposeHostsAsync (:155), plus the optional hooks OnContainersStartedAsync (:161) and ConfigureSharedEnvironment (:170).
      • SqlServerBaseConnectionString (:79-81) throws a clear InvalidOperationException when the container has not started, and the public static ComposeConnectionString(...) (:91-105) overlays a catalog, TrustServerCertificate, and an optional Application Name. It is deliberately pure and static so a fixture's connection-string composition is unit-testable with no Docker daemon (:83-90); BuildConnectionString (:177-178) is the instance shorthand over it.
      • InitializeAsync (:108-125) is the whole lifecycle in seven steps: create the containers, start both in parallel with Task.WhenAll (:111), read the broker connection string (:113), run the subclass hook (:114), pre-create the databases (:120), push the shared environment (:122), then boot the hosts (:124). The pre-create step carries the sharpest comment in the file (:116-119): CREATE DATABASE runs before EF's migration lock (sp_getapplock) is acquired, so a host booted twice (the real-Kestrel double-boot pattern) would otherwise race itself; with the databases already present EF skips the create and the migration lock serializes the actual migration run.
      • SetSharedEnvironment (:236-272) pushes ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT=Testing (:238), one named data source per module (:252-255), the real broker settings MessageBus__Provider=RabbitMq and ConnectionStrings__rabbitmq (:258-259), the shared Application__Namespace (:264), and the dummy Bearer authority that only has to exist so AddForwardedJwtBearer's authority guard passes (:269; real validation is re-pointed at the committed test key by JwtTokenGenerator.ConfigureInProcessTokenValidation, :266-268), before handing control to the subclass (:271). The namespace comment (:261-263) gives the reason: the hosts are services of ONE application, so they share the prefix every broker topic carries; a broker host refuses to start without it, and each host's own application name would put every service on topics of its own. ConfigureSharedEnvironment may override it.
      • The named-source loop is the multi-host fix, and its comment (:240-251) is worth reading in full: EF Core caches a context type's model in a process-global cache keyed by (context type, source name). If every host let its entities collapse onto Default (as production does, one host per process), all hosts here would share ONE cached model and the first booted would win. SetNamedDataSource (:279-290) therefore composes each module's connection string with a distinct Application Name MMCA-{LogicalName} (:284) so it differs ordinally from the top-level ConnectionStrings value and the resolver keeps the named source, giving each host its own model-cache key.
      • SetHostConnectionString (:186-187) is the one key mutated between sequential boots, and SetEnvironmentVariable (:196-204) records only the first original value per key so re-pushing that key cannot clobber the restore point. DisposeAsync (:128-145) disposes the hosts, then RabbitMQ, then SQL, then calls RestoreEnvironment (:292-300).
      • CreateContainers (:212-213) is built inside a method rather than a field initializer so a subclass can be constructed and its non-container logic unit-tested on a machine with no Docker daemon, and it carries a documented CS0618 suppression for the parameterless Testcontainers module builders, which are [Obsolete] in Testcontainers 4.11 and later (:206-211). CreateDatabasesAsync (:216-234) issues one guarded IF DB_ID(...) IS NULL CREATE DATABASE per source with a scoped CA2100 suppression justified because the database names are the subclass's own compile-time constants (:227).
    • Why it's built this way: the environment-variable channel and the sequential boot are not style choices, they are the only way to give several hosts distinct databases in one process given configure-time configuration reads. Everything genuinely per-app (which databases, how many hosts and in what order, which extra settings) stays behind the four abstract members.
    • Where it's used: one fixture per app, both sealed subclasses, MMCA.ADC/Tests/Integration/MMCA.ADC.CrossService.IntegrationTests/Infrastructure/CrossServiceFixture.cs:24 (three databases for three REST hosts at :61-66, migrations prefix MMCA.ADC.Migrations.SqlServer at :69) and MMCA.Store/Tests/Integration/MMCA.Store.CrossService.IntegrationTests/Infrastructure/CrossServiceFixture.cs:29 (two databases at :56-60, prefix MMCA.Store.Migrations.SqlServer at :63). MMCA.Common covers the container-free half of the base through its own private FakeCrossServiceFixture (MMCA.Common/Tests/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Tests/Fixtures/CrossServiceFixtureBaseTests.cs:119).
    • Caveats / not-in-source: this tier needs a Docker daemon. Where each repo schedules it is a CI decision recorded outside this class; the base itself says nothing about scheduling. It also proves the round-trip over RabbitMQ, not the production transport, which is what ServiceBusEmulatorFixtureBase exists to cover.

    DecoratorPipelineOrderTestsBase<TCommand, TCommandResult, TQuery, TQueryResult>

    MMCA.Common.Testing · MMCA.Common.Testing.Conformance · MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing/Conformance/DecoratorPipelineOrderTestsBase.cs:38 · Level 1 · class (abstract)

    • What it is: an opt-in fitness function that builds a real ServiceCollection through a repo's own registration sequence, resolves the decorated command and query handlers out of the built provider, and asserts the runtime object graph nests the decorators in exactly the ADR-014 order.
    • Depends on: ICommandHandler<in TCommand, TResult> and IQueryHandler<in TQuery, TResult> from MMCA.Common.Application.UseCases (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing/Conformance/DecoratorPipelineOrderTestsBase.cs:4), plus System.Reflection, Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection, AwesomeAssertions, and Xunit (:1-5).
    • Concept introduced, verifying a decorator chain by unwrapping the constructed graph. The decorator pipeline itself is taught in group-05; what is new here is how you prove it. Scrutor's TryDecorate applies decorators in reverse registration order, so the outermost decorator is the last one registered, and an innocent-looking reorder of the AddApplicationDecorators() lines (or a module scan that runs after it) silently changes runtime behavior with no compile error (class doc, MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing/Conformance/DecoratorPipelineOrderTestsBase.cs:16-19). Rather than inspecting the registration list, this base resolves the service and walks the real chain by reflection (:29-32). [Rubric §6, CQRS & Event-Driven] assesses whether the command/query pipeline is coherent and intentional; [Rubric §2, Design Patterns] assesses correct application of the decorator pattern; [Rubric §14, Testability] covers turning an ordering convention into an executable check; and [Rubric §34, Architecture Governance & Documentation] covers the fact that a decision record is enforced here rather than merely written down (ADR-015 is the general case). It is also the one non-HTTP member of the ADR-058 conformance tier.
    • Walkthrough
      • Four type parameters (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing/Conformance/DecoratorPipelineOrderTestsBase.cs:34-37): a representative command with its TResult and a representative query with its TResult, each of which must have a concrete registered handler.
      • ConfigureServices(IServiceCollection services) (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing/Conformance/DecoratorPipelineOrderTestsBase.cs:46): the one abstract member. The subclass registers test doubles for the decorator dependencies (IFeatureManager, ICurrentUserService, IPermissionRegistry, ICorrelationContext, ICacheService, IUnitOfWork, ILogger<>) and then runs the repo's real registration sequence, module scans first and AddApplicationDecorators() last (doc :20-28).
      • ExpectedCommandDecorators (:49-59) pins eight links, outermost first: ViewAsCommandDecorator<TCommand, TResult> (:51, the read-only guard for a caller holding a view-as token), FeatureGateCommandDecorator<TCommand, TResult>, AuthorizationCommandDecorator<TCommand, TResult>, LoggingCommandDecorator<TCommand, TResult>, CachingCommandDecorator<TCommand, TResult>, ValidatingCommandDecorator<TCommand, TResult>, TimeoutCommandDecorator<TCommand, TResult>, TransactionalCommandDecorator<TCommand, TResult>. ExpectedQueryDecorators (:62-70) pins six: FeatureGateQueryDecorator<TQuery, TResult>, AuthorizationQueryDecorator<TQuery, TResult>, LoggingQueryDecorator<TQuery, TResult>, CachingQueryDecorator<TQuery, TResult>, ValidatingQueryDecorator<TQuery, TResult>, TimeoutQueryDecorator<TQuery, TResult>, the query pipeline differing from the command one by the absence of the view-as guard at the outer end and the transaction at the inner end (class doc, :14-16). Both lists are virtual, so a host with a deliberately different chain can narrow them.
      • The two [Fact]s, CommandPipeline_NestsDecorators_InAdr014Order (:72-74) and QueryPipeline_NestsDecorators_InAdr014Order (:76-78), each hand the closed handler interface and the expected list to AssertPipeline.
      • AssertPipeline (:80-99): builds the collection, builds a provider, opens a scope (handlers are scoped, :85-86), resolves the outermost handler and asserts it is non-null with a message that tells the subclass author what is missing (:88-90). It then unwraps the chain, maps each link to a simple type name, and asserts every element except the last equals the expected decorator list in order (:92-95), finally asserting the innermost element does not end in Decorator, that is, it is the concrete handler (:97-98).
      • UnwrapChain (:106-126): walks outermost to innermost by reflecting over each object's instance fields (public and non-public) and picking the first value that implements the same closed handler interface and is not the object itself (:113-116), which is how it finds the compiler-generated backing field holding the inner handler. SimpleTypeName (:128-133) strips the generic-arity backtick suffix so a two-arity LoggingCommandDecorator compares as the plain name.
    • Why it's built this way: asserting the constructed object graph is strictly stronger than asserting the registration list, it catches a decorator that was registered but never applied (for example because a module scan re-registered the handler afterwards). Comparing simple type names keeps the base free of a compile-time reference to the decorator classes, which live in MMCA.Common.Application.
    • Where it's used: four subclasses today. MMCA.Common self-tests the base against its own registration sequence with a synthetic PingCommand / PingQuery pair (MMCA.Common/Tests/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Tests/Conformance/DecoratorPipelineOrderTests.cs:24), and the three applications subclass it in their architecture tiers, MMCA.ADC/Tests/Architecture/MMCA.ADC.Architecture.Tests/Cqrs/DecoratorPipelineOrderTests.cs:30 and MMCA.Store/Tests/Architecture/MMCA.Store.Architecture.Tests/Cqrs/DecoratorPipelineOrderTests.cs:30 over the real Identity ChangePreferencesCommand / GetUserPreferencesQuery pair, and MMCA.Helpdesk/Tests/Architecture/MMCA.Helpdesk.Architecture.Tests/DecoratorPipelineOrderTests.cs:35 over the Tickets pair.
    • Caveats / not-in-source: each subclass pins one representative command/query pair, not every handler, so the guard proves the ordering is right, not that every handler is decorated.

    • What it is: a private nested decorator over IEntityConfigurationAssemblyProvider that narrows the assemblies a host scans for entity configurations to the ones that host would load in its own process. It is the working half of CrossServiceHostIsolation.IsolateCrossServiceHost<TEntryPoint>(), the extension that CrossServiceFixtureBase subclasses call from ConfigureTestServices of every host factory (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing/Fixtures/CrossServiceHostIsolation.cs:10-13,42).

    • Concept introduced, scoping a shared AppDomain back to one host. The default provider scans AppDomain.GetAssemblies, and with several hosts in one process that returns every host's module assemblies. Each host's entity registry then claims its peers' data sources, so its outbox and internal-command processors drain the PEER databases and a row whose handler lives only in the peer is dead-lettered as handler_missing by the wrong host (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing/Fixtures/CrossServiceHostIsolation.cs:14-21). The provider restores the one-service-per-process view. [Rubric §7, Microservices Readiness] assesses whether extracted services behave as independent hosts; [Rubric §8, Data Architecture] covers database-per-service (ADR-006); [Rubric §14, Testability] covers keeping the in-process topology faithful to deployment.

      • The primary constructor takes the wrapped inner provider, the hostAssemblyNames set, and the explicitAssemblies collection (:116-119).

ReadHostAssemblyNames (:79-114) reads every runtime library the host's .deps.json lists plus the host assembly itself, and throws InvalidOperationException when the file is missing beside the assembly (:86-91). IsolateCrossServiceHost removes the existing non-keyed registrations (:47-53), reuses the last as inner (:55), and registers this class as a singleton (:56-59); CreateInner (:65-73) rebuilds the original from its descriptor, falling back to DefaultEntityConfigurationAssemblyProvider.
    • Why it's built this way: decorating rather than replacing keeps whatever provider the host registered and only narrows its result. Explicit AdditionalAssemblies bypass the filter because that registration is already per host (:23-28).

    InMemoryQueryableExecutor

    MMCA.Common.Testing · MMCA.Common.Testing.Support · MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing/Support/InMemoryQueryableExecutor.cs:16 · Level 1 · class

    • What it is: a no-op, in-memory stand-in for the framework's IQueryableExecutor, the interface that carries the EF Core-specific parts of query execution (eager loading, split queries, materialization) out of application code. This implementation lets a unit test build the same query pipeline against a plain IQueryable<T> (an in-memory list, typically) with no EF Core provider in play at all.
    • Depends on: IQueryableExecutor (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing/Support/InMemoryQueryableExecutor.cs:16), the interface it implements, plus BCL LINQ only (System.Linq). No EF Core reference.
    • Concept introduced, the null-object executor. [Rubric §14, Testability] assesses how cheaply application code can be exercised without its infrastructure; a handler or service that takes IQueryableExecutor as a dependency stays unit-testable because a test can hand it this no-op instead of standing up a real DbContext. Every member either returns the query unchanged or runs the equivalent synchronous LINQ operator, so the executor adds no behavior of its own, it exists purely to satisfy the interface's shape over a query that is already fully in memory.
    • Walkthrough
      • Include<T>(IQueryable<T> query, string navigationPropertyPath) (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing/Support/InMemoryQueryableExecutor.cs:19-21): returns query unchanged, an in-memory collection has no navigation properties left to load.
      • AsSplitQuery<T>(IQueryable<T> query) (:24-26): likewise a pass-through, split-query behavior is an EF Core query-translation concern with nothing to do once the sequence is already materialized.
      • ToListAsync<T>(IQueryable<T> query, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default) (:29-30): wraps the synchronous query.ToList() in Task.FromResult, so an await at the call site still works with no real asynchrony underneath.
      • CountAsync<T>(IQueryable<T> query, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default) (:32-33): the same pattern over query.Count().
    • Why it's built this way: keeping every member a one-line pass-through or a synchronous LINQ call wrapped in Task.FromResult is what makes the type safe to reuse across every test that needs an IQueryableExecutor, there is no state to reset between tests and no behavior that could diverge from what an in-memory IQueryable<T> already does on its own.
    • Where it's used: as the IQueryableExecutor handed to application-layer tests across both apps and the framework itself, for example MMCA.ADC/Tests/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Application.Tests/Helpers/TestSupport.cs, .../SessionQuestions/UseCases/GetModerationQueueHandlerTests.cs, .../SessionQuestions/UseCases/GetSessionQuestionsHandlerTests.cs, .../LivePolls/DomainEventHandlers/LivePollVoteChangedHandlerTests.cs, .../LivePolls/Services/LivePollResultsBuilderTests.cs, .../LivePolls/UseCases/CastVoteHandlerTests.cs, .../LivePolls/UseCases/GetOpenPollsHandlerTests.cs, .../LivePolls/UseCases/GetPollResultsHandlerTests.cs, .../SessionQuestions/UseCases/SubmitQuestionHandlerTests.cs, MMCA.ADC/Tests/Modules/Notification/MMCA.ADC.Notification.Application.Tests/UserNotificationExportServiceTests.cs, MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Application.Tests/Services/Query/EntityQueryServiceTests.cs, and .../Services/Query/EntityQueryPipelineOrderingTests.cs, plus one more site not shown in the brief's usage-site slice.

    • What it is: the workhorse base class every integration test inherits. It owns the per-test HTTP client and lifecycle, typed request helpers, bearer-token management, and a thread-safe id counter, so a concrete test class is left with just its arrange/act/assert.
    • Depends on: IIntegrationTestFixture (the TFixture constraint, MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing/Fixtures/IntegrationTestBase.cs:13), plus Xunit's IAsyncLifetime, System.Net.Http.Headers, and System.Net.Http.Json (:1-3).
    • Concept introduced, the xUnit async test lifecycle and per-test isolation. [Rubric §14, Testability]: the base implements IAsyncLifetime so InitializeAsync runs before each test and DisposeAsync after, and it hangs the database reset off that hook so every test starts from a clean database, the single most important property for reliable integration tests.
    • Walkthrough
      • Fields and properties: a static int _nextId = 1000 seed (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing/Fixtures/IntegrationTestBase.cs:15), and the Fixture / Client protected properties (:19-22).
      • Constructor (:24-28): stores the injected fixture and eagerly creates the HttpClient from it.
      • InitializeAsync (:31): a ValueTask that awaits Fixture.ResetDatabaseAsync() before each test. DisposeAsync (:34-39): suppresses finalization and disposes the client.
      • Auth helpers: SetBearerToken(string) / ClearAuthentication() (:42-48) set or clear the Authorization header, the hook through which a JwtTokenGenerator token is applied.
      • Typed HTTP helpers: GetAsync<T> (:51-56, which calls EnsureSuccessStatusCode then deserializes), and PostAsync<T> / PutAsync<T> / PutAsync / DeleteAsync (:59-72) returning the raw HttpResponseMessage so a test can assert status codes. The four write helpers are plain expression-bodied pass-throughs returning the client's Task directly (no async/await wrapper), while GetAsync<T> stays async because it awaits twice.
      • NextId() (:75): Interlocked.Increment over the shared seed, so parallel tests never collide on generated ids.
    • Why it's built this way: per-test database reset plus a per-test client is the isolation contract; centralizing the typed helpers keeps individual tests short and consistent. The static Interlocked counter is the cheapest safe way to hand out unique ids under xUnit's parallelism. Note the asymmetry: GetAsync<T> throws on a non-success status while the others hand the response back, which is what makes a read helper terse and a write assertion explicit.
    • Where it's used: the direct base of all three contract test bases in this unit (OpenApiContractTestsBase<TFixture>, ProblemDetailsContractTestsBase<TFixture>, ServiceInfoVersioningContractTestsBase<TFixture>), and of every concrete integration test in the downstream apps.

[Rubric §9, API & Contract Design]: a sealed positional record gives value equality for free, which is exactly what lets the detector collect findings in a HashSet<OpenApiBreakingChange> (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing/Conformance/OpenApiBreakingChangeDetector.cs:73) and report a shared component once instead of once per reference site.

    RecordingHttpForwarder

    MMCA.Common.Testing · MMCA.Common.Testing.Support · MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing/Support/RecordingHttpForwarder.cs:29 · Level 1 · sealed class

    • What it is: an IHttpForwarder that never proxies. It echoes the destination prefix, the matched cluster, and the ForwarderRequestConfig it was handed into response headers, so a gateway test can assert which cluster a route targets and which forwarder budget it carries (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing/Support/RecordingHttpForwarder.cs:8-13).
    • Depends on: YARP only, Yarp.ReverseProxy.Forwarder (IHttpForwarder, ForwarderRequestConfig, HttpTransformer, ForwarderError) and Yarp.ReverseProxy.Model (IReverseProxyFeature), plus Microsoft.AspNetCore.Http and System.Globalization (:1-4). No first-party dependency. The trace headers it reads back are the ones the gateway kit's GatewayTraceHeaderTransformProvider stamps. The Yarp.ReverseProxy package reference lives in MMCA.Common.Testing itself rather than in every gateway test project, and the project file records why (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing/MMCA.Common.Testing.csproj:43-46).
    • Concept introduced, the echoing fake at a framework extension point. Three ideas are worth taking from this type. First, echoing into response headers rather than storing state is what keeps a singleton fake safe for concurrent requests (:12-13): there is no shared mutable field to race. Second, replacing the DI singleton still intercepts under a config-driven route table, because YARP's own forwarder middleware resolves IHttpForwarder from DI, so MapReverseProxy() goes through the fake exactly as a hand-written MapForwarder call would (:14-22). Third, it runs the real transform pipeline against a throwaway outbound request before echoing (:23-27), so the request transforms are observable without a network hop, which is what makes an assertion about what a downstream would actually receive meaningful. [Rubric §2, Design Patterns] covers the test-double form (a recording fake, not a mock); [Rubric §14, Testability] covers keeping every gateway test off the network, since configured destinations are usually service-discovery names that resolve to nothing in a test host; and [Rubric §7, Microservices Readiness] is the topology this makes testable (ADR-089).
    • Walkthrough
      • Header constants (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing/Support/RecordingHttpForwarder.cs:32-54): DestinationHeader, ClusterHeader, ActivityTimeoutHeader, VersionHeader, VersionPolicyHeader, plus RouteTraceEchoHeader and ClusterTraceEchoHeader for the two trace headers read back off the transformed outbound request. UnsetValue (:57) is the (unset) marker written when the forwarder config leaves a nullable setting unset, so a test asserts a value either way rather than distinguishing an absent header from an unset setting.
      • RouteTraceHeaderName (:63) and ClusterTraceHeaderName (:69): init properties defaulting to the shared kit's own header names, X-MMCA-Route and X-MMCA-Cluster, so a host with different header names can still use the fake.
      • The five-argument SendAsync overload (:72-78) simply delegates to the six-argument one with CancellationToken.None.
      • The real SendAsync (:81-115): null-guards context, config and transformer (:89-91); writes the destination prefix (:93); reads the matched cluster id off IReverseProxyFeature, falling back to UnsetValue (:94-95); writes the activity timeout, forwarded HTTP version and version policy (:96-101); runs transformer.TransformRequestAsync against a throwaway HttpRequestMessage (:106-108); echoes the two stamped trace headers (:110-111); then sets a 200 and returns ForwarderError.None (:113-114).
      • HeaderOrUnset (:121-124): reads one outbound header, joining multiple values with a comma, or returns the unset marker.
    • Why it's built this way: a gateway test wants to assert routing decisions and forwarder budgets, not the behavior of a backend. Swapping the forwarder is the smallest replacement that leaves the entire gateway pipeline (routing, transforms, limiter, correlation, health) genuinely running, which is what makes the same fixture reusable for both the route-map assertions and the hardening gates.
    • Where it's used: both gateway test projects register it by replacing the singleton. ADC uses it in the gateway-hardening fixture (MMCA.ADC/Tests/Hosts/MMCA.ADC.Gateway.Tests/GatewayHardeningTests.cs:104) and in the route-map suite, which aliases all seven header constants at the top of the class (MMCA.ADC/Tests/Hosts/MMCA.ADC.Gateway.Tests/RouteMapTests.cs:43-61, registration at :430); Store does the same in both places (MMCA.Store/Tests/Hosts/MMCA.Store.Gateway.Tests/GatewayHardeningTests.cs:115, MMCA.Store/Tests/Hosts/MMCA.Store.Gateway.Tests/RouteMapTests.cs:378, with the rationale written out at :21). MMCA.Common covers the fake itself, including the unset-marker paths and the custom trace header names (MMCA.Common/Tests/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Tests/Support/RecordingHttpForwarderTests.cs:17).

    GracefulShutdownTestsBase<TEntryPoint>

    MMCA.Common.Testing · MMCA.Common.Testing.Conformance · MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing/Conformance/GracefulShutdownTestsBase.cs:25 · Level 1 · class (abstract)

    • What it is: a shutdown conformance base. It boots a real host, calls a real IHost.StopAsync under a bounded cancellation token, and asserts the host drained cleanly, firing ApplicationStopping and then ApplicationStopped inside the timeout.
    • Depends on: ProductionHostApplicationFactory<TEntryPoint> (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing/Conformance/GracefulShutdownTestsBase.cs:32), plus Microsoft.Extensions.Hosting's IHost / IHostApplicationLifetime, Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection, AwesomeAssertions, and Xunit (:1-4).
    • Concept introduced, the bounded-stop drain check. [Rubric §29, Resilience & Business Continuity] (named in the class doc itself, MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing/Conformance/GracefulShutdownTestsBase.cs:10) assesses whether the system survives planned and unplanned interruption; a rolling deploy is the planned one. The failure this catches is a hosted service (a warm-up runner, service discovery, proxy infrastructure) that refuses to drain, which in production does not announce itself: it silently wedges a rolling deploy while the platform waits out its termination grace period (:13-17). [Rubric §13, Observability & Operability] is the operational half, lifetime events firing in order are what a platform's shutdown handling depends on. The recovery-objective framing is ADR-009; the base itself is one of the suites recorded in ADR-058.
    • Walkthrough
      • ShutdownTimeoutSeconds (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing/Conformance/GracefulShutdownTestsBase.cs:29): virtual, defaults to 20 seconds. This number is the test: a host that drains slower than this fails.
      • CreateFactory() (:31): virtual, returns a plain ProductionHostApplicationFactory<TEntryPoint>. The doc says to override it only when the host needs a fixture beyond a Production-pinned boot (:18-21).
      • Host_StopsGracefully_FiringLifetimeEventsWithinTimeout (:33-62): the single [Fact]. It creates the factory (:36) and holds the disposal as a separate ConfiguredAsyncDisposable (:40), with an inline comment explaining why (:38-39): the shorter await using var factory = ....ConfigureAwait(false) form would retype factory and lose access to CreateClient and StartedHost.
      • It then creates and immediately disposes a client (:42-45), which is what forces the lazy host to build and start, asserts StartedHost is non-null (:47-48), resolves IHostApplicationLifetime (:49), and confirms ApplicationStarted already fired (:50).
      • The stop itself (:55-56): a CancellationTokenSource for ShutdownTimeoutSeconds and await host.StopAsync(timeout.Token). Reaching the next line already means the stop returned cleanly inside the budget, because a wedged hosted service makes the token cancel and StopAsync throw (:52-54).
      • The two closing assertions (:58-61): ApplicationStopping must have fired during the shutdown, and ApplicationStopped must signal once the host has fully stopped, each with its own because-reason.
    • Why it's built this way: the bounded token is the mechanism, not decoration. Without it a host that never drains would hang the test run instead of failing it, which is exactly the production symptom the test exists to surface. Driving a real IHost.StopAsync (rather than asserting registrations) is what makes this a runtime check.
    • Where it's used: both gateways, each a body-less one-line subclass, MMCA.Store/Tests/Hosts/MMCA.Store.Gateway.Tests/GracefulShutdownTests.cs:9 and MMCA.ADC/Tests/Hosts/MMCA.ADC.Gateway.Tests/GracefulShutdownTests.cs:9. Both run in the no-database host-test tier, so they are in each repo's CI.slnf.

    Comparison

    MMCA.Common.Testing · MMCA.Common.Testing.Conformance · MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing/Conformance/OpenApiBreakingChangeDetector.cs:61 · Level 2 · class (private sealed, nested)

    • What it is: the private worker nested inside OpenApiBreakingChangeDetector. One instance holds the two parsed roots (baseline and live), the collected findings, and the set of schema pairs already visited, and walks the baseline looking for what the live document dropped or tightened (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing/Conformance/OpenApiBreakingChangeDetector.cs:61).
    • Depends on: System.Text.Json (JsonElement), OpenApiBreakingChange and OpenApiBreakingChangeKind, plus two private records, OperationSite (:497) and ParameterSite (:511).
    • Concept introduced, a baseline-driven structural diff. [Rubric §9, API & Contract Design]: the walk iterates the BASELINE and looks each thing up in the live document, so additions are never even visited. That one-sided direction is what makes "additive changes pass" a property of the algorithm, not a filter.
    • Walkthrough
      • State: OperationNames (:63, the eight HTTP methods), _visited (:65), a private Direction enum of Request / Response (:67-71), and the Changes set (:73).
      • ComparePaths (:75): per baseline path, RemovedPath if gone; per baseline operation, RemovedOperation if gone, otherwise it builds an OperationSite and runs the three comparisons below.
      • CompareParameters (:260): parameters are keyed by location and name, name case-insensitive, via EffectiveParameters (:224), where an operation's own parameters override its path item's. Emits RemovedParameter, ParameterNewlyRequired and AddedRequiredParameter; CompareParameterSchema (:301) adds ChangedParameterType. A path parameter is always required (ParameterSite.IsRequired, :514).
      • CompareRequestBody (:326): RemovedRequestBody, AddedRequiredRequestBody (only when the live body carries required: true), RemovedRequestMediaType, then the content is compared in the request direction.
      • CompareResponses (:381): RemovedResponseStatusCode, otherwise content compared in the response direction. CompareContent (:403) then CompareSchema (:423).
      • CompareSchema (:423): resolves $refs, skips a pair already in _visited (which also stops recursive schemas, :433-437), reports ChangedPropertyType when the declared type sets differ (DeclaredTypes, :133, drops the null type first, :152, so nullability is not a type change), then recurses through properties and items.
      • CompareProperties (:455): a baseline property missing from live is RemovedResponseProperty only in the response direction; in the request direction a property newly in required is RequestPropertyNewlyRequired (:484-493).
      • Helpers: Escape (:116, RFC 6901 ~0/~1), TryGetObject (:119), Resolve (:169, follows local #/ refs with a 32-hop cap, :171), TryNavigate (:189).
    • Why it's built this way: direction matters. A caller breaks when a request property becomes required; a reader breaks when a response property disappears; a type change breaks both. Pointers move with $ref resolution so a finding names the component, not the reference site.
    • Where it's used: instantiated once per Detect call (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing/Conformance/OpenApiBreakingChangeDetector.cs:52).
    • Caveats / not-in-source: only local #/ references are followed; external refs are left unresolved and the pair is compared as written.

    CrossServiceHostIsolation

    MMCA.Common.Testing · MMCA.Common.Testing.Fixtures · MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing/Fixtures/CrossServiceHostIsolation.cs:30 · Level 2 · static class

    • What it is: a static extension on IServiceCollection that narrows one in-process test host to its own modules. Its single entry point, IsolateCrossServiceHost<TEntryPoint>() (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing/Fixtures/CrossServiceHostIsolation.cs:42), replaces the host's IEntityConfigurationAssemblyProvider with a filtering wrapper so its registry, outbox, internal-command and cleanup processors only enumerate that host's data sources.
    • Depends on: IEntityConfigurationAssemblyProvider, DefaultEntityConfigurationAssemblyProvider and EntityConfigurationOptions (its AdditionalAssemblies are kept regardless of the filter), plus the host's .deps.json. It is the isolation half of CrossServiceFixtureBase, whose class doc names it as the call every host factory makes from ConfigureTestServices (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing/Fixtures/CrossServiceFixtureBase.cs:43).
    • Concept introduced, host isolation by dependency manifest. [Rubric §14, Testability]: when several hosts share one test process, the default AppDomain scan hands each host its peers' module assemblies and, through the per-module DataSources__{X} keys, its peers' databases, so each host's outbox would drain them all (CrossServiceFixtureBase.cs:40-44). The runtime closure of a host is exactly what its .deps.json lists, so filtering the scanned assemblies to that closure reproduces production's one-host-one-module-set shape (ADR-006). The method is declared in an extension(IServiceCollection services) block, the public DI-surface style of ADR-106.
    • Walkthrough
      • IsolateCrossServiceHost<TEntryPoint> (:42-62): reads the host's assembly names (ReadHostAssemblyNames), removes every non-keyed IEntityConfigurationAssemblyProvider descriptor (:47-53), remembers the last one as the inner provider, and registers a singleton HostScopedAssemblyProvider wrapping it (:56-59); returns the collection for chaining.
      • CreateInner (:65-73): rebuilds the removed registration by shape (none registered gives DefaultEntityConfigurationAssemblyProvider via ActivatorUtilities, then instance, factory or implementation type), throwing InvalidOperationException for any other shape.
      • ReadHostAssemblyNames (:79-114): takes the host assembly name plus the file name of every runtime entry under every targets library in the .deps.json beside the assembly (:93-111); throws InvalidOperationException when the file is missing (:86-91).
      • HostScopedAssemblyProvider (:116-126): keeps an inner assembly only if it is in the explicit AdditionalAssemblies set or its simple name is in the host's name set.
    • Why it's built this way: the manifest is the authoritative closure and needs no per-host allow-list, so a new module reference flows in automatically. Reading it requires the file beside the assembly, which WebApplicationFactory copies for every referenced host project (:89-90).
    • Where it's used: called from CrossServiceFixtureBase (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing/Fixtures/CrossServiceFixtureBase.cs:43) and covered by MMCA.Common/Tests/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Tests/Fixtures/CrossServiceHostIsolationTests.cs.

    SqlServerIntegrationTestFixtureBase<TEntryPoint>

    MMCA.Common.Testing · MMCA.Common.Testing.Fixtures · MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing/Fixtures/SqlServerIntegrationTestFixtureBase.cs:27 · Level 2 · class (abstract)

    • What it is: the reusable fixture that boots a real service host in-process against a throwaway SQL Server database, applies the module's migrations on first start, resets data between tests with Respawn, and drops the database on disposal. It is the concrete engine behind IIntegrationTestFixture for SQL Server hosts.
    • Depends on: IIntegrationTestFixture (implemented, MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing/Fixtures/SqlServerIntegrationTestFixtureBase.cs:27), CrossServiceFixtureBase (its static ComposeConnectionString helper, MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing/Fixtures/CrossServiceFixtureBase.cs:91), plus Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Testing (WebApplicationFactory), Microsoft.Data.SqlClient, Respawn, and Xunit's IAsyncLifetime (:1-4).
    • Concept introduced, the disposable-database integration fixture and environment-variable overrides. [Rubric §14, Testability] and [Rubric §8, Data Architecture]: real integration coverage needs a real relational database, and this fixture makes that cheap and hermetic, a fresh GUID-named database per fixture, migrated from scratch, Respawned between tests, dropped at the end. The database-per-service routing (ADR-006) is why the class doc stresses the DataSources collapse onto a single overridden connection string (:16-24).
    • Walkthrough
      • State (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing/Fixtures/SqlServerIntegrationTestFixtureBase.cs:30-45): the recorded original-environment map, the server-base and database-name strings, the WebApplicationFactory, the Respawner, a _databaseCreated flag, and the public Client / ConnectionString. ConnectionString (:45) is exposed so SQL-fidelity tests can read raw tables (for example to assert an integration event landed in the outbox).
      • Services (:52): the booted host's root service provider, exposed so cross-service tests can resolve a consumer-side integration-event handler or a repository and drive the flow directly against the real database.
      • Abstract knobs: SqlBaseEnvironmentVariable (:58, names the env var holding the CI SQL base connection string), DatabaseNamePrefix (:61), and CreateFactory() (:134, where the subclass builds the host). CreateClient() (:64) satisfies the interface by delegating to the factory.
      • InitializeAsync (:67-101): resolves the server base from SqlBaseEnvironmentVariable or falls back to LocalDB (:69-70), composes a GUID-suffixed database name (:71) and builds the connection string through CrossServiceFixtureBase.ComposeConnectionString (:72), which overlays the catalog on the base string with a SqlConnectionStringBuilder and forces TrustServerCertificate (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing/Fixtures/CrossServiceFixtureBase.cs:91-97), forces ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT=Testing and pushes the top-level SQL connection string as environment variables (:75-76), lets the subclass push its own via ConfigureTestEnvironment (:77), and builds the factory (:79). It then sets _databaseCreated = true (:85) before creating the client, because the flag means "may exist", not "exists": the drop is guarded by IF DB_ID(...), so dropping a never-created database is a no-op, while a host that fails after its migration created the database still has it dropped instead of leaking it on the shared server (:81-85). Creating the client is what triggers the host's Migrate init to create the database and apply the module's migrations (:87-89). It then builds the Respawner, ignoring __EFMigrationsHistory (:91-100).
      • ResetDatabaseAsync (:104-117): returns immediately when no respawner exists, otherwise opens a connection and calls Respawner.ResetAsync.
      • DisposeAsync (:120-136): disposes client and factory, drops the database when the flag is set, and restores the environment.
      • ConfigureTestEnvironment (:147-149) is an empty virtual hook receiving the setter delegate. SetEnvironmentVariable (:151-160) records only the first original value per key so re-pushing a key cannot clobber the restore point; RestoreEnvironment (:162-170) puts them all back and clears the map.
      • DropDatabaseAsync (:172-193): clears pooled connections so the database is free to drop (:175), connects to master through the same ComposeConnectionString helper (:177), and runs an IF DB_ID(...) IS NOT NULL guarded SET SINGLE_USER WITH ROLLBACK IMMEDIATE plus DROP DATABASE (:185-188), with a scoped CA2100 suppression justified because the database name is a server-generated GUID, never user input (:184).
    • Why it's built this way: overrides go through process environment variables because the host reads its connection string at configure-time; forcing the Testing environment skips appsettings.Development.json (which would point DataSources at localhost) so the resolver collapses onto the single overridden top-level connection string, making the fixture behave like a clean single-database monolith. LocalDB-by-default keeps local runs zero-config while CI can point at a SQL service container. Note the contrast with CrossServiceFixtureBase, which needs the opposite (named sources per host so several EF models can coexist in one process); the two fixtures nevertheless share one pure, static connection-string composer, so the catalog overlay is identical in both and unit-testable without a container (CrossServiceFixtureBase.cs:83-91).
    • Where it's used: the base of every per-service integration fixture in both apps, four in ADC (MMCA.ADC/Tests/Integration/MMCA.ADC.Conference.IntegrationTests/Infrastructure/ConferenceIntegrationTestFixture.cs:18, .../MMCA.ADC.Engagement.IntegrationTests/Infrastructure/EngagementIntegrationTestFixture.cs:18, .../MMCA.ADC.Identity.IntegrationTests/Infrastructure/IdentityIntegrationTestFixture.cs:23, .../MMCA.ADC.Notification.IntegrationTests/Infrastructure/NotificationIntegrationTestFixture.cs:18) and three in Store (MMCA.Store/Tests/Integration/MMCA.Store.Catalog.IntegrationTests/Infrastructure/CatalogIntegrationTestFixture.cs:16, .../MMCA.Store.Identity.IntegrationTests/Infrastructure/IdentityIntegrationTestFixture.cs:16, .../MMCA.Store.Sales.IntegrationTests/Infrastructure/SalesIntegrationTestFixture.cs:17). Each is then the TFixture for that service's integration and contract tests.
    • Caveats / not-in-source: the fixture needs a reachable SQL Server, so these suites build but do not run without one; they execute in each repo's SQL-service CI job via the *.Integration.slnf filter.

    OpenApiBreakingChangeDetector

    MMCA.Common.Testing · MMCA.Common.Testing.Conformance · MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing/Conformance/OpenApiBreakingChangeDetector.cs:38 · Level 3 · static class

    • What it is: a pure function over two OpenAPI JSON strings. Detect(baselineJson, liveJson) returns only the changes that break an existing client (removed path, operation, status code, parameter, request body or media type; newly required property, parameter or body; removed response property; changed type) and passes everything else (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing/Conformance/OpenApiBreakingChangeDetector.cs:44-58).
    • Depends on: System.Text.Json and System.Globalization (:1-2), the private nested Comparison worker, and the OpenApiBreakingChange record with its OpenApiBreakingChangeKind enum (thirteen members, MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing/Conformance/OpenApiBreakingChangeKind.cs:4-44).
    • Concept introduced, structural rather than textual contract comparison. [Rubric §9, API & Contract Design]: both documents are read by member name, so property order never shows up as a change, and only the contract-bearing members are read (paths, parameters, in, name, responses, requestBody, content, schema, $ref, type, properties, required, items), so descriptions, summaries, examples and tags are ignored by construction (:14-22). This is the machinery behind the baseline opt-in described in ADR-058.
    • Walkthrough
      • Detect (:44-58): guards both arguments with ArgumentException.ThrowIfNullOrWhiteSpace (:46-47), parses with JsonDocument (:49-50), runs Comparison.ComparePaths (:52-53), and returns the findings ordered by pointer (ordinal) then kind (:55-57), so the report is deterministic.
      • Everything else lives in Comparison (:61-519).
    • Why it's built this way: a static, dependency-free function is trivially unit-testable against hand-written documents, which is how the framework tests it (MMCA.Common/Tests/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Tests/Conformance/OpenApiBreakingChangeDetectorTests.cs and OpenApiBreakingChangeDetectorParameterTests.cs); the contract base only supplies the two strings.
    • Where it's used: called by OpenApiContractTestsBase<TFixture>.OpenApiDocument_HasNoBreakingChangesAgainstTheBaseline (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing/Conformance/OpenApiContractTestsBase.cs:149) and see OpenApiContractTestsBase<TFixture>.

A subclass supplies the host's TenancySettings and inherits three facts that must stay true: header resolution is an explicit opt-in, the signed claim wins over the header, and the health probes bypass tenant resolution (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing/Conformance/TenantResolutionTestsBase.cs:27-101).

      • Knobs: ProbePaths (:30, /health and /alive), abstract Settings (:33), virtual AllowsHeaderResolution (:40, default false).

    OpenApiContractTestsBase<TFixture>

    MMCA.Common.Testing · MMCA.Common.Testing.Conformance · MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing/Conformance/OpenApiContractTestsBase.cs:32 · Level 4 · class (abstract)

    • What it is: a contract conformance base that boots a host and asserts its /openapi/v1.json document is served, is a well-formed OpenAPI 3.x document, and still describes the core public resources, so an accidental controller or route removal fails CI instead of silently changing the published contract.
    • Depends on: IntegrationTestBase<TFixture> (inherited, MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing/Conformance/OpenApiContractTestsBase.cs:32), System.Net, System.Text.Json, AwesomeAssertions, and Xunit (:1-4), plus OpenApiBreakingChangeDetector for the opt-in baseline test.
    • Concept introduced, the contract guard on the live document. [Rubric §9, API & Contract Design] assesses whether the API surface is described and kept stable; the default of all three contract bases is a live-document guard with no committed snapshot (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing/Conformance/OpenApiContractTestsBase.cs:15-17), the assertions run against the document the host actually serves, so new controllers can never leave a stale snapshot behind and a removed one is caught immediately. A subclass can additionally opt in to a committed baseline diff that fails only on breaking changes. This is one of the suites recorded in ADR-058, and the one with the widest adoption.
    • Walkthrough
      • Overridable and abstract knobs: OpenApiDocumentPath (:51, defaults to /openapi/v1.json), MinimumPathCount (:58, a coarse floor under the route surface), MinimumPathCountBecause (:65, the failure-message reason), CorePublicResources (:71, the resource paths that must keep being described), and BaselineDocumentPath (:80, null by default, which turns the baseline test into a no-op).
      • RefreshBaselineEnvironmentVariable (:41, "MMCA_UPDATE_OPENAPI_BASELINE"): the public constant that switches the baseline test into refresh mode; the private IndentedOptions (:43) indents the rewritten file.
      • OpenApiDocument_IsServed_AsWellFormedOpenApiDescribingTheApiSurface (:82-95): parses the JSON and asserts openapi starts with 3., info.title is non-empty, a paths object exists, and it holds at least MinimumPathCount entries.
      • OpenApiDocument_DescribesEveryCorePublicResource (:98-115): first guards against a vacuous pass (the subclass must pin at least one resource, :100-101), then checks every CorePublicResources entry is present, matching on name case-insensitively (:107-110) so presence, not exact casing, is the contract.
      • OpenApiDocument_HasNoBreakingChangesAgainstTheBaseline (:118-159): returns immediately when BaselineDocumentPath is null (:120-124), sending no request at all. With the variable set to 1 it rewrites the baseline from the live document (indented, :131-132) and then fails on purpose (:135-140), so a regenerating run can never pass in CI. Otherwise it asserts the baseline file exists (:143), runs OpenApiBreakingChangeDetector.Detect (:149) and requires zero changes, listing each one plus the RefreshGuidance text (:176).
      • GetOpenApiJsonAsync (:165-174): clears auth (the document is anonymous outside Production), fetches the path, asserts 200 with a message naming the path, and returns the raw JSON. Indent (:180) re-serializes the document for a line-by-line diffable baseline.
    • Why it's built this way: asserting the live document by default keeps the guard maintenance-free while still catching the two failures that matter, the document disappearing and a public resource vanishing; the two assertions are deliberately coarse because a strict shape diff would fail on every ordinary additive change. Hosts that want a stricter contract opt in to the baseline, whose detector ignores additive and documentation-only changes, so the gate fires only on what breaks a client.
    • Where it's used: subclassed once per REST service host, four in ADC (MMCA.ADC/Tests/Integration/MMCA.ADC.Conference.IntegrationTests/Contract/OpenApiContractTests.cs:16, .../MMCA.ADC.Engagement.IntegrationTests/Contract/OpenApiContractTests.cs:15, .../MMCA.ADC.Identity.IntegrationTests/Contract/OpenApiContractTests.cs:16, .../MMCA.ADC.Notification.IntegrationTests/Contract/OpenApiContractTests.cs:17) and three in Store (MMCA.Store/Tests/Integration/MMCA.Store.Catalog.IntegrationTests/Contract/OpenApiContractTests.cs:15, .../MMCA.Store.Identity.IntegrationTests/Contract/OpenApiContractTests.cs:15, .../MMCA.Store.Sales.IntegrationTests/Contract/OpenApiContractTests.cs:15), each supplying the fixture, the path floor, and the pinned resource list.

It runs the shared ViewAsGrantLogQuery.Filter over _grants.AsQueryable() and clamps with the same PagingMath.Clamp call (:73-74), so a test of the grant log exercises the same filter, ordering and clamp the database path uses (the remark at :65), and a filter change cannot pass in the fake while failing against SQL. Support access by view-as is recorded in ADR-137 (cited by the class doc, :9).

      • Backing state: the private _grants list (:15), exposed read-only as Grants in insertion order (:18); Seed(ViewAsGrant) (:22) places an already-persisted grant.

[Rubric §14, Testability]: ConfigureWebHost is sealed (:52-57), so a subclass cannot skip or reorder the defaults; it gets two virtual hooks instead. The class doc fixes the order (:17-23): environment, the RequireHttpsMetadata setting, ConfigureHost, then one test-services callback that re-points the bearer scheme, neutralizes the limiter and finally calls ConfigureTestServices. Because that callback runs after the host's own registrations, a fake registered in the hook wins.       • TestingEnvironmentName (:35): the public constant "Testing".
      • Audience (:43): virtual, null by default. When set, the Bearer scheme is re-pointed at the committed test key; null leaves the scheme alone, which suits an Identity host that validates its own tokens (:37-42).
      • RateLimiterPartitionName (:49): virtual, defaults to "integration-tests"; null leaves the global limiter untouched.

    InMemoryRefreshSessionStore

    MMCA.Common.Testing · MMCA.Common.Testing.Support · MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing/Support/InMemoryRefreshSessionStore.cs:27 · Level 7 · sealed class

    • What it is: an in-memory IRefreshSessionStore fake for handler and application-service unit tests, giving a test both a seedable list of already-persisted sessions and a staged-insert buffer that only lands on the seeded list once SaveChangesAsync runs, so a test can assert what a handler wrote without a database.
    • Depends on: IRefreshSessionStore (implemented, MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing/Support/InMemoryRefreshSessionStore.cs:27) and RefreshSession (:29-30), the identifier alias UserIdentifierType, and System.Threading for CancellationToken.
    • Concept introduced, the stage-then-flush fake. Rather than mutate a single backing list on every call, the fake keeps two lists: _staged (:29) for rows an in-flight unit of work has added but not yet saved, and _sessions (:30) for what a real store would already have durably persisted. AddAsync (:63-67) only appends to _staged; only SaveChangesAsync (:194-201) moves the staged rows onto _sessions and increments SaveCount (:196). This mirrors the two-phase add-then-SaveChangesAsync contract every IUnitOfWork-backed repository has, so a test exercising a handler that forgets to call SaveChangesAsync sees the session absent from Sessions, the same gap a real database would show. [Rubric §14, Testability] is the fit: no database, no host, and the fake still models the commit boundary rather than eagerly persisting on every write.
    • Walkthrough
      • Backing state (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing/Support/InMemoryRefreshSessionStore.cs:29-30): the private _staged and _sessions lists. Sessions (:33) exposes _sessions read-only, in insertion order. SaveCount (:36) counts how many times the store was flushed.
      • RotationOutcome (:43): an optional Func<bool> a test sets to force TryRotateAsync to report a lost race, standing in for the database arbitrating two concurrent rotations of the same token where the loser writes nothing (doc :39-41).
      • Seeding helpers: Seed(RefreshSession) (:47) drops an already-built session straight onto _sessions, bypassing the staged path; SeedLive(userId, token, createdAt, expiresAt) (:55-60) builds one via RefreshSession.Create(...).Value! and seeds it, for a test that only has raw field values rather than a session in hand.
      • AddAsync (:63-67): stages the session; FindByTokenHashAsync (:70-71) does an ordinal-equality scan over _sessions (never _staged) by token hash; GetUnrevokedByUserAsync (:74-87) filters _sessions by user id and !IsRevoked, ordering by CreatedAt then Id to match the real store's contract; FindByIdAsync (:178-183) scans _sessions by id and user id together; FindByIdUntrackedAsync (:190-191) scans _sessions by id alone. The real store uses it to read past a tracked copy, but this fake has no tracked copy to see past (every read hands out the one persisted instance, which already reflects any rotation), so the "fresh" read returns the same instance.
      • Session-administration reads, all over _sessions only: GetAllByUserAsync (:90-103) returns every session for a user including revoked ones, ordered by CreatedAt then Id (the unfiltered counterpart of GetUnrevokedByUserAsync); GetRecentSignInsAsync (:111-142) folds the same answer the EF store computes in SQL (remark :106-110) into RefreshSessionSignIn entries: it rejects a non-positive maxSignIns (:116), groups the user's sessions by SignInId into one entry per chain carrying the earliest CreatedAt and the newest row by (CreatedAt, Id) (:120-126), adds each row with no SignInId whose ReasonRevoked is not RefreshSession.ReasonRotated as its own entry (:128-131), then orders by StartedAt then SignInId descending and takes the cap (:133-139); GetUserIdsWithLiveSessionsAsync (:145-158) returns the distinct owner ids of sessions where IsActiveAt(now) holds; CountLiveSessionsByUserAsync (:161-175) null-guards userIds, then groups the active sessions of the requested users into a per-user count (users with no live session are absent from the dictionary).
      • SaveChangesAsync (:194-201): increments SaveCount, moves every staged row onto _sessions, clears _staged, and returns the count written.
      • TryRotateAsync (:204-227): null-guards both sessions (:210-211); consults RotationOutcome to simulate a lost race (:213-216); calls presented.Revoke(revokedAt, RefreshSession.ReasonRotated, successor.TokenHash) and bails out on failure (:218-221); on success, stages the successor and immediately flushes via AddAsync plus SaveChangesAsync (:223-224), so a caller sees the successor in Sessions without a separate save call.
    • Why it's built this way: the staged/persisted split is what lets a test distinguish "the handler called AddAsync" from "the handler's unit of work actually committed," which is exactly the bug class the framework's SaveChangesAsync-returns-1-by-default convenience (HandlerTestBase<THandler>) is meant to catch for other aggregates. FindByTokenHashAsync only ever sees _sessions, never _staged, so an uncommitted add is invisible to a lookup, matching how a real store would behave mid-transaction.
    • Where it's used: seeded and asserted against directly in two ADC suites, MMCA.ADC/Tests/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.Application.Tests/Users/AuthenticationServiceTests.cs (3 references) and .../MMCA.ADC.Identity.Application.Tests/Speakers/IntegrationEventHandlers/SpeakerLinkedToUserHandlerTests.cs (2), and across MMCA.Common suites, most heavily MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Application.Tests/Auth/Sessions/AuthSessionIssuerLostResponseRecoveryTests.cs (9), MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Application.Tests/Auth/RefreshSessionRevocationTests.cs (3), MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Application.Tests/Auth/SignIn/SignInTestDoubles.cs (3), MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Application.Tests/Users/DeleteUserHandlerBaseTests.cs (3), MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Application.Tests/Users/UseCases/ExportUserData/RefreshSessionUserDataExportSectionTests.cs (3), MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Application.Tests/Auth/AuthenticationServiceBaseTests.cs (2) and MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Application.Tests/Auth/RefreshSessionManagementTests.cs (2), with its own coverage in MMCA.Common/Tests/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Tests/Support/InMemoryRefreshSessionStoreTests.cs; more than a dozen further suites reference it once or twice.

    MiddlewarePipelineOrderTestsBase

    MMCA.Common.Testing · MMCA.Common.Testing.Conformance · MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing/Conformance/MiddlewarePipelineOrderTestsBase.cs:31 · Level 11 · class (abstract)

    • What it is: the HTTP-edge counterpart of DecoratorPipelineOrderTestsBase<TCommand, TCommandResult, TQuery, TQueryResult>. It seeds the framework's default middleware step list, applies the host's own customization if it has one, and asserts the resulting step order is exactly the documented pipeline, plus that the startup-validated adjacency invariants still hold.
    • Depends on: MiddlewarePipelineBuilder and MiddlewarePipelineStepNames from MMCA.Common.API.Startup.Pipeline (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing/Conformance/MiddlewarePipelineOrderTestsBase.cs:2), plus AwesomeAssertions and Xunit (:1,3). This is the reference that makes MMCA.Common.Testing depend on MMCA.Common.API (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing/MMCA.Common.Testing.csproj:44-46).
    • Concept introduced, order-as-data at the HTTP edge. In ASP.NET Core middleware order is behavior, not style, and the failures it produces do not look like ordering bugs. The class doc pins four adjacencies and names two runtime failures they guard against (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing/Conformance/MiddlewarePipelineOrderTestsBase.cs:13-17): a tenant that never resolves when tenant resolution runs before authentication, and a per-user rate cap that never engages when the limiter runs before authentication. It is explicit that the third adjacency, the pre-forwarded capture immediately before UseForwardedHeaders, has no runtime consequence today: nothing in the framework reads the captured Items, and the OIDC discovery endpoint derives jwks_uri from Jwt:Issuer, so that adjacency is pinned as structure only (:17-19). What makes the check cheap is that ADR-079 turned the order into data: MiddlewarePipelineBuilder.CreateDefault() produces a list of named steps that are inert until applied, so no WebApplication has to be built and the test runs in the fast unit tier with no database and no host (:27-28). [Rubric §17, DevOps & Deployment] assesses whether cross-cutting edge concerns are composed deliberately; [Rubric §11, Security] is why authentication before the rate limiter is load-bearing (ADR-019); [Rubric §14, Testability] and [Rubric §34, Architecture Governance & Documentation] cover the fitness-function form itself (ADR-015).
    • Walkthrough
      • Configure (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing/Conformance/MiddlewarePipelineOrderTestsBase.cs:37): virtual, defaults to null, meaning the host under test calls the zero-argument UseCommonMiddlewarePipeline() overload. A host that customizes the pipeline overrides this with the same Action<MiddlewarePipelineBuilder> its Program.cs passes (:22-24).
      • ExpectedStepNames (:39-61): the pinned order, outermost first, all nineteen steps named through MiddlewarePipelineStepNames constants rather than string literals: ExceptionHandler, CorrelationId, RequestLocalization, PreForwardedCapture, ForwardedHeaders, HttpsRedirection, ResponseCompression, Routing, Cors, Authentication, TenantResolution, RateLimiting, SoftDeletedUserFilter, ViewAsGuard, Authorization, OutputCache, JwksEndpoint, OidcDiscoveryEndpoint, Controllers. ViewAsGuard (:55), the step that applies ViewAsGuardMiddleware, sits after the soft-deleted-user filter and before authorization, matching the framework default (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Startup/Pipeline/MiddlewarePipelineBuilder.cs:127). It is virtual, so a host with a deliberately different pipeline states its own order.
      • EdgePipeline_OrdersSteps_InDocumentedOrder (:63-70): the first [Fact]. It builds the seeded builder and asserts builder.StepNames equals ExpectedStepNames, with a because-reason (:69) that spells out three adjacencies rather than just reporting a list mismatch: the pre-forwarded capture immediately before UseForwardedHeaders so the captured pre-forwarded scheme and host stay faithful, tenant resolution immediately after authentication so the claim strategy sees HttpContext.User, and the rate limiter after authentication per ADR-019 so the per-user cap engages.

Build() (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Startup/Pipeline/MiddlewarePipelineBuilder.cs:260-283) re-checks four invariants at startup, PreForwardedCapture immediately before ForwardedHeaders (:262-265), Authentication immediately before TenantResolution (:267-270), Authentication before RateLimiting (:272-275), and ForwardedHeaders before HttpsRedirection (:277-280), so a pipeline that fails here would have thrown while the host was starting.
      • CreateBuilder (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing/Conformance/MiddlewarePipelineOrderTestsBase.cs:82-87): the two-line private helper both facts share, MiddlewarePipelineBuilder.CreateDefault() followed by Configure?.Invoke(builder).
    • Why it's built this way: the two facts are complementary rather than redundant. The first pins the exact order, so any reorder (including one that still satisfies every adjacency) fails visibly; the second re-runs the host's own startup validation in the unit tier, so an override that breaks an adjacency fails in a test rather than at boot. Naming steps through MiddlewarePipelineStepNames constants means a step rename is a compile error in the test rather than a silent string mismatch.
    • Where it's used: four subclasses, every one of them body-less because every host calls the zero-argument overload, MMCA.Common/Tests/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Tests/Conformance/MiddlewarePipelineOrderTests.cs:12, MMCA.ADC/Tests/Architecture/MMCA.ADC.Architecture.Tests/Api/MiddlewarePipelineOrderTests.cs:16, MMCA.Store/Tests/Architecture/MMCA.Store.Architecture.Tests/Api/MiddlewarePipelineOrderTests.cs:16, and MMCA.Helpdesk/Tests/Architecture/MMCA.Helpdesk.Architecture.Tests/MiddlewarePipelineOrderTests.cs:15. The framework's own UseCommonMiddlewarePipeline doc points back at this base as the way to freeze the order (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Startup/WebApplicationExtensions.cs:45).

Where IntegrationTestBase<TFixture> gives an end-to-end test a booted host, this gives an isolated unit test a mocked persistence boundary: no database, no host, no HTTP. The class doc (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing/Support/HandlerTestBase.cs:10-12) frames it as the shared replacement for the per-test copy-paste of Mock<IUnitOfWork> plus GetRepository wiring plus SaveChangesAsync setup. [Rubric §14, Testability] assesses whether the design permits fast isolated tests; the fact that handlers depend on IUnitOfWork (an Application-layer abstraction) rather than a DbContext is what makes this scaffold possible at all, which is [Rubric §3, Clean Architecture] paying off in the test tier (ADR-055 records that contract). [Rubric §15, Best Practices & Code Quality] covers the deduplication itself.

      • UnitOfWork (:45): the Mock<IUnitOfWork> every registered repository is wired into, created by a property initializer so the constructor can configure it.
      • Logger (:48): NullLogger<THandler>.Instance, typed by the handler type parameter so it binds directly to the handler's ILogger<THandler> constructor parameter.
      • RegisterRepository<TEntity, TIdentifierType>() (:56-64): creates a Mock<IRepository<TEntity, TIdentifierType>>, wires that same object into both GetRepository<...>() and GetReadRepository<...>() (:61-62), and returns the mock for further Setup / Verify. Constrained to AuditableAggregateRootEntity<TIdentifierType> (:57), that is, to aggregate roots.

Pre-succeeding SaveChangesAsync encodes the common case so only the interesting deviation appears in a test.
