    AnonymousEndpointTestsBase

    MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture · MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture · MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture/Bases/Api/AnonymousEndpointTestsBase.cs:30 · Level 0 · abstract class

    • What it is: an allow-list gate for authorization opt-outs. Every [AllowAnonymous] in the assemblies a subclass names, and every base read a [PublicCachedReads] controller opens, must appear in an explicit, reviewed list, so an endpoint cannot quietly lose its authorization gate. A second gate, on by default and opt-out per repo, closes the complementary hole: an endpoint carrying no authorization attribute at all.
    • Depends on: [Fact] (xUnit), AwesomeAssertions, RuleHelpers.LoadableTypes, and reflection over attribute instances matched by full name: AllowAnonymousAttribute, AuthorizeAttribute, ControllerBase, Blazor's RouteAttribute and the framework's own PublicCachedReadsAttribute are five private full-name constants (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture/Bases/Api/AnonymousEndpointTestsBase.cs:32-36), not compile-time references.
    • Concept introduced, the two-directional allow-list gate. A one-directional "no anonymous endpoints" rule is unusable (login has to be anonymous) and a one-directional "these are allowed" rule rots. This base asserts both halves: no unlisted [AllowAnonymous] exists, and no list entry matches nothing. The second half is the subtle one, since a stale entry hides a renamed or re-gated endpoint behind a permission that is no longer being granted (reason string, line 118). [Rubric §11, Security] assesses whether authentication gates stay where they were put; [Rubric §14, Testability] assesses turning a review-only property into an executable one; [Rubric §34, Architecture Governance] applies because the exception list, with its per-entry justification comments, becomes the reviewed record of the anonymous surface.
    • Walkthrough
      • The subclass supplies TargetAssemblies (line 42), AllowedAnonymousEndpoints (line 49, identified as the type's FullName for a type-level attribute and FullName.MethodName for a method-level one, lines 45-47), and a MinimumScannedTypes floor (line 56, default 1).
      • Three allow-list [Fact]s. AnonymousEndpoints_AreAllowListed (line 84) subtracts the allow-list from the discovered set and names what is left. ScannedEndpointSet_IsNotEmpty (line 96) is the non-vacuity guard: with no controllers and no routable components discovered, the first assertion passes without having looked at anything (comment, lines 98-99). AllowList_HasNoStaleEntries (line 109) runs the comparison the other way.
      • Two shapes are scanned, both by reflection: IsController (line 163) walks the base chain for ControllerBase, and IsRoutableComponent (line 179) looks for RouteAttribute on the type, combined in IsScannedEndpointType (line 157).
      • AnonymousEndpoints() (line 187) is protected rather than private so a subclass can build a richer report over the same data (doc, lines 182-186); it flattens the assemblies, filters to the scanned shapes, and returns a distinct, ordinally-ordered set.
      • AnonymousEndpointsOf (line 263) is the load-bearing detail: type-level attributes are read with inherit: false (line 265) and methods are enumerated DeclaredOnly (line 285), so a framework base action is reported once at its declaration site instead of once per derived controller in every consumer repo (comment, lines 283-284).
      • A type that itself carries [PublicCachedReads] (tested by HasPublicCachedReads, line 260) yields three identifiers, {FullName}.GetAllAsync, {FullName}.GetAllForLookupAsync and {FullName}.GetByIdAsync, from the private PublicCachedReadActionNames array (line 39; both GetAllAsync overloads share one identifier, doc line 38), emitted at lines 275-281. They are the identifiers an attribute-only [AllowAnonymous] override of those reads produces, so an existing allow-list stays valid, and because only the type's own attribute is read, an inherited one is reported once, at the base that declares it (comment, lines 272-274).
      • The undecorated-endpoint gate is enforced by default: RequireExplicitAuthorizationDecision (line 73) returns true, and its companion list EndpointsWithoutAuthorizationAttribute (line 81) defaults to empty. Endpoints_DeclareAnAuthorizationDecision (line 123) fails any undecorated endpoint not in that companion list (lines 131-137). A repo that is not ready overrides the flag to false, and the fact then returns immediately without checking anything (lines 125-129). UndecoratedAllowList_HasNoStaleEntries (line 141) is that list's own stale-entry guard, the same shape as AllowList_HasNoStaleEntries, and runs regardless of the flag.
      • UndecoratedEndpoints() (line 203) mirrors AnonymousEndpoints() but selects concrete types with no decision at all: a controller or routable component counts as decided when the type, any type it inherits from, or any public action declared along that chain carries [Authorize] (HasPermissionAttribute derives from it), [AllowAnonymous] or [PublicCachedReads] (doc, lines 195-202). UndecoratedEndpointsOf (line 211) skips abstract types on purpose, since the concrete controller inheriting the action set is where the decision belongs, and reports per type rather than per action, because a controller that forgot [Authorize] usually declares no method of its own (comment, lines 213-217). DeclaresAuthorizationAnywhere (line 233) walks the base-type chain checking both the type and its declared methods; HasAuthorizationAttribute (line 254) is the shared three-attribute test both reduce to.
    • Why it's built this way: the class doc is explicit about the limit (lines 18-24). Minimal-API endpoints opt out through the .AllowAnonymous() builder call, which produces endpoint metadata at map time and is invisible to static reflection, so the framework's own minimal-API anonymous surface (JWKS, OIDC discovery, app-association, session-cookie refresh, health) is outside this gate; catching it would need an endpoint-metadata check over a built host. Matching ASP.NET types by full name keeps the package free of an ASP.NET reference, the same stance the whole rule library takes (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture.csproj:22-29). The stricter gate defaults on (line 73; doc lines 58-64): the allow-list check alone cannot see an endpoint carrying no authorization attribute at all, exactly the shape a forgotten [Authorize] produces, so a repo must decline it explicitly by overriding the flag to false rather than adopt it by remembering to. On a controller ASP.NET Core's fallback authorization policy closes that hole at run time, but AuthorizeRouteView gates a routable Blazor component by reading attributes and ignoring the fallback policy entirely, so for pages this test IS the control (remarks, lines 65-72). Treating [PublicCachedReads] as both an anonymous opening and an authorization decision means a public cached-read controller needs no hand-written override just to carry [AllowAnonymous], while every read it opens still lands in the reviewed allow-list. ADR context: Website/docs-src/adr/020-permission-based-authorization.md.
    • Where it's used: subclassed in all four repos, and the DeclaredOnly and own-attribute decisions are what keep each list local to what that repo declares. MMCA.Common's AnonymousEndpointTests lists the credential-exchange actions on its controller bases (MMCA.Common/Tests/Architecture/MMCA.Common.Architecture.Tests/Api/AnonymousEndpointTests.cs:14, list at :22, floor of 21 at :91). ADC's covers the Identity credential actions plus the public conference-browse reads, calendar exports and bookmark counts, with a floor of 85 (MMCA.ADC/Tests/Architecture/MMCA.ADC.Architecture.Tests/Api/AnonymousEndpointTests.cs:23, list at :35, floor at :149). Store's covers the public storefront reads, product images, registration and the Stripe webhook, with a floor of 38 (MMCA.Store/Tests/Architecture/MMCA.Store.Architecture.Tests/Api/AnonymousEndpointTests.cs:10, floor at :135). Helpdesk's lists its whole TicketsController, because the seed ships without an Identity issuer so there is no token to require (MMCA.Helpdesk/Tests/Architecture/MMCA.Helpdesk.Architecture.Tests/AnonymousEndpointTests.cs:17, entry at :30, floor of 3 at :42). MMCA.Common also carries the adversarial coverage for the base itself in AnonymousEndpointTestsBaseTests, which proves each assertion fails on its own drift through private subclasses (DriftedTests, StaleAllowListTests, EmptyScanTests, StrictDriftedTests and StaleUndecoratedAllowListTests at MMCA.Common/Tests/Architecture/MMCA.Common.Architecture.Tests/Api/AnonymousEndpointTestsBaseTests.cs:222, :230, :239, :248, :258) plus conformant controls (:269, :284), and pins the [PublicCachedReads] behavior with PublicCachedReadsType_YieldsThreeReadIdentifiers (:134) and PublicCachedReadsType_CountsAsAuthorizationDecision (:154) over direct, declaring-base and inheriting fixture controllers (:168, :175, :181).

The header body may be plain (= {), conditional (= if (cond) {), looped (= [for x in xs: {) or both (= [for x in xs: if (cond) {), so an optional or per-item container app is checked rather than skipped (comment, lines 104-108).

Drift in any of the three throws nothing: it silently reorders registration, leaves a module permanently enabled, or swaps a real service for a disabled stub. That is exactly the failure class a fitness function exists for. [Rubric §7, Microservices Readiness] assesses whether module boundaries and their declared dependencies stay honest as modules move between hosts; [Rubric §14, Testability] assesses whether a silent contract is made loud; [Rubric §34, Architecture Governance] applies because the module contract is enforced rather than described. Module_ShouldDeclare_ExpectedName (line 39) compares the read Name, with a because spelling out the consequence: renaming silently disables the module's configuration and drops it from other modules' dependency graphs (line 42). Module_ShouldDeclare_ExpectedDependencies (line 45) casts the value to IEnumerable<string>, asserts it is not null (the shape ModuleLoader sorts on, lines 49-50), then BeEquivalentTo the expectation (lines 52-54). Module_ShouldDeclare_ExpectedRequiresDependencies (line 58) pins the flag that turns a disabled dependency into a startup failure instead of a substituted stub (line 61). Module_ShouldRegister_ExpectedDisabledStubs (line 64) delegates to the AssertDisabledStubs hook.
      • AssertDisabledStubs (line 77) is deliberately empty by default: a module exporting no cross-module contract registers no stubs, so the fact passes vacuously and only a module that does export one overrides it (doc, lines 70-76).
      • The private ReadContractMember (line 81) is the load-bearing mechanism. It finds the IModule interface on the instance by full-name match (lines 85-87), asserts the module implements it at all (lines 89-90), resolves the named public instance property off the interface (line 92), and reads it (line 99). Reading through the interface property dispatches to the module's override when there is one and to the framework's default interface implementation when there is not (comment, lines 97-98).

    MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture · MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture · MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture/Bases/Governance/ObservabilityConventionTestsBase.cs:30 · Level 0 · abstract partial class

    • What it is: an SLO alert-to-runbook pairing gate. It parses the SLO metric alerts a consumer's infra/main.bicep provisions and asserts each one keeps a matching, severity-correct triage section in that repo's infra/OPERATIONS.md, in both directions: a missing runbook section fails, and so does an orphan runbook section whose alert no longer exists. A fourth check, on by default, additionally requires the bicep to provision an operator-facing monitoring view (an Azure Monitor workbook or a portal dashboard) next to those alerts.
    • Depends on: System.Globalization, source-generated System.Text.RegularExpressions regexes, Assembly.GetManifestResourceStream, AwesomeAssertions, and [Fact] (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture/Bases/Governance/ObservabilityConventionTestsBase.cs:1-2). No first-party dependency and, notably, no IArchitectureMap: it reads embedded text, not assemblies.
    • Concept introduced, the documentation-pairing gate. [Rubric §13, Observability & Operability] assesses whether an operator paged at 3am has usable guidance; the failure mode this base closes is the silent one, an alert added, renamed, or re-tiered while its runbook section stays behind. [Rubric §17, DevOps] applies because the source of truth is the IaC template itself, and [Rubric §34, Architecture Governance] because it makes the "every alert has a runbook" convention executable rather than aspirational.
    • Walkthrough
      • Overridable knobs: MinimumAlertSpecs (line 39, default 3), the two manifest-resource logical names BicepResource (line 42, infra.main.bicep) and RunbookResource (line 45, infra.OPERATIONS.md), and ResourceAssembly (line 51), which defaults to GetType().Assembly. A fifth knob, RequireWorkbook (line 60), defaults to true: an alert an operator cannot look at the signal behind is half a monitoring story, so every consumer gets the check without opting in. A subclass overrides it to false only for a deployment that deliberately has no operator-facing view, and says why in the override.
      • MonitoringWorkbookOrDashboard_IsProvisioned_WhenRequired (lines 67-79) returns immediately when RequireWorkbook is off; otherwise it asserts MonitoringViewResourceRegex finds at least one resource declaration of type Microsoft.Insights/workbooks or Microsoft.Portal/dashboards in the bicep (line 77), so the signals the alerts fire on also have a place an operator can look at them.
      • SloAlertSpecs_AreDiscovered_GateIsNotVacuous (lines 81-89) is the honesty guard: discovering fewer specs than the floor means the parse anchors drifted, not that alerts disappeared.
      • EveryProvisionedSloAlert_HasASeverityCorrectRunbookSection (lines 91-117) matches each alert key against the runbook headings through HeadingNamesAlert (line 101, built on the -alert- infix constant at line 32) and then asserts the heading also carries the (sev N) tag matching the bicep severity (lines 108-112).
      • EveryRunbookAlertSection_MapsToAProvisionedAlert (lines 119-131) is the reverse direction, flagging stale guidance, and reads headings through the same predicate (line 126).
      • HeadingNamesAlert (lines 156-178, protected static) is the one shared pairing predicate. It matches -alert-{key} as a whole token: an optional -v{digits} version suffix is allowed, then the heading must end, or continue with whitespace, ( or a closing backtick (regex at line 175, 2 second timeout). Any other hyphenated continuation is a different alert, so the section for server-response-time-p99 cannot answer for server-response-time, and an orphan x-extra section cannot hide behind a surviving x alert, as a plain substring test would have allowed.
      • DiscoverAlertSpecs (lines 133-154) slices the bicep between var sloAlertSpecs and resource sloAlerts (lines 137-140, each index assertion carrying its own because), runs AlertKeyRegex and AlertSeverityRegex over that block, and asserts the two match counts agree (line 145) so a changed spec shape fails loudly instead of silently mis-pairing. DiscoverRunbookAlertHeadings (line 180) keeps only the ### headings carrying the infix. The four [GeneratedRegex] partial properties sit at lines 191-201, each with a 2000 ms match timeout; the last, MonitoringViewResourceRegex (lines 200-201), is multiline and case-insensitive.
      • ReadEmbedded (lines 182-189) throws a message naming the assembly when a resource is missing.
    • Why it's built this way: the class doc (lines 23-28) records why the ResourceAssembly default is load-bearing. The base ships inside the framework package, so resolving resources against its own assembly would look for the consumer's bicep inside MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture.dll and always throw. Defaulting to the derived type's assembly means a subclass needs no wiring beyond two EmbeddedResource entries in its csproj (the snippet is in the doc at lines 18-22).
    • Where it's used: subclassed in ADC (MMCA.ADC/Tests/Architecture/MMCA.ADC.Architecture.Tests/Governance/ObservabilityConventionTests.cs:7), where the single override raises MinimumAlertSpecs from the base default of three to six (:14) so the gate cannot pass vacuously on a drifted parse, and in Store (MMCA.Store/Tests/Architecture/MMCA.Store.Architecture.Tests/Governance/ObservabilityConventionTests.cs:7), whose one override raises the floor to five (:13); see ObservabilityConventionTests. Neither overrides RequireWorkbook, so both inherit the default true and their bicep must provision a workbook or dashboard. MMCA.Common subclasses it twice. ObservabilityConventionTestsBaseTests is a deliberate cross-assembly guard that repoints both resource names at local fixtures (MMCA.Common/Tests/Architecture/MMCA.Common.Architecture.Tests/Governance/ObservabilityConventionTestsBaseTests.cs:14, resources at :16-18) and adds one extra [Fact] pinning the ResourceAssembly default to the derived type's assembly rather than the base's (:24-29). Block is never produced by TryPushScope: the statement loop pushes an anonymous Block scope itself when a statement that is not a scope header ends with { (lines 161-166), so the block's closing brace pops that scope rather than the enclosing message or service.

    • What it is: an abstract test base that reflects over a UI assembly's routable Blazor pages and fails the build if a page the subclass marks as governed has lost its [Authorize(Roles = "...")] role gate.
    • Depends on: [Fact] (xUnit), AwesomeAssertions, RuleHelpers.LoadableTypes, and pure reflection over attribute instances matched by full name (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture/Bases/Api/RouteAuthorizationTestsBase.cs:24-25).
    • Concept introduced, the security-regression fitness function. [Rubric §11, Security] and [Rubric §25, Navigation & IA] assess whether protected routes stay protected; this base turns "the admin page must require the Organizer role" from a review checklist into a compiled assertion, so a page cannot silently regress from a role-scoped [Authorize] to a bare [Authorize] reachable by any authenticated user. It is the page-level counterpart to AnonymousEndpointTestsBase, which guards the opt-out side of the same question.
    • Walkthrough
      • The subclass supplies TargetAssembly (line 28), the exact RequiredRole (line 31), an IsGovernedPage strategy (line 40), and a MinimumGovernedPages non-vacuity floor (line 47, default 1).
      • GovernedPages_RequireDeclaredRole (line 50) collects pages that are routable, governed, and do not require the role, then asserts the offender set is empty, naming each offender's route templates (lines 52-60).
      • GovernedPageSet_IsNotEmpty (line 64) guards the guard: if a refactor moved namespaces so IsGovernedPage matched nothing, the first test would pass vacuously, so this one asserts the discovered count meets the floor (lines 68-73).
      • Detection is all reflection by attribute full name: IsRoutablePage (line 77), RequiresRole (line 86, which reads the Roles property off every AuthorizeAttribute instance, own and inherited, and passes when any one requires the exact role by ordinal match, so a bare [Authorize] or a different role alone fails; the attribute allows multiple instances and ASP.NET Core enforces all of them, so a policy-only sibling or a derived page's bare [Authorize] cannot hide the role gate, and the result no longer depends on which instance reflection returns first), the subclass helper HasAuthorizeAttribute (line 97), Routes (line 100), and the base-type walk IsOrDerivesFrom (line 108) that lets a derived authorize attribute still count.
    • Why it's built this way: matching attributes by full name keeps the shared package free of an ASP.NET Core reference (lines 16-20) while still inspecting ASP.NET attributes; the package's only dependencies are AwesomeAssertions and the xUnit extensibility core (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture.csproj:16-17). A reflection scan also covers future pages matching the strategy without hand-enumeration. Deliberately anonymous public pages and bare-[Authorize] self-service pages simply must not match IsGovernedPage (lines 12-15).
    • Where it's used: subclassed per module UI test project, five times today: MMCA.ADC/Tests/Modules/Conference/MMCA.ADC.Conference.UI.Tests/ManagementRouteAuthorizationTests.cs:26, MMCA.ADC/Tests/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.UI.Tests/IdentityRouteAuthorizationTests.cs:16, and Store's Catalog, Sales, and Identity equivalents (MMCA.Store/Tests/Modules/Catalog/MMCA.Store.Catalog.UI.Tests/CatalogRouteAuthorizationTests.cs:15, MMCA.Store/Tests/Modules/Sales/MMCA.Store.Sales.UI.Tests/SalesRouteAuthorizationTests.cs:18, MMCA.Store/Tests/Modules/Identity/MMCA.Store.Identity.UI.Tests/IdentityRouteAuthorizationTests.cs:15).

    RuleHelpers

    MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture · MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture · MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture/RuleHelpers.cs:15 · Level 0 · internal static class

    • What it is: the internal reflection toolbox the reflection-based fitness functions share: extension members for enumerating loadable types, matching suffix conventions on generic types, detecting base types and interfaces by open generic or name prefix, and classifying property setters as mutable or init-only.
    • Depends on: System.Reflection (Assembly, Type, PropertyInfo, ReflectionTypeLoadException, BindingFlags) only.
    • Concept introduced: the doc (lines 5-10) states the premise: the metadata dependency rules answer one question, which types a type names, so the rules about method return types, generic-argument constraints, property accessors or attribute usage reflect over loaded types directly through these helpers. [Rubric §14, Testability] and [Rubric §15, Best Practices & Code Quality] apply: the reflection subtleties (partial assembly loads, init-only detection) are solved once here rather than re-derived per rule.
    • Walkthrough: the class body is three C# preview extension(T) blocks, so every helper is an extension property or method, not a classic this-parameter extension method (the syntax is taught in primer §4).
      • extension(Assembly assembly) (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture/RuleHelpers.cs:17): LoadableTypes (line 19) tolerates a partially-resolvable assembly by catching ReflectionTypeLoadException and returning the types that did load through OfType<Type>(), which both filters nulls and narrows the element type (lines 27-31). ConcreteClasses (line 36) narrows that to non-abstract classes. Classes (line 45) returns every class including abstract ones (interfaces still excluded), for rules whose subject can legitimately be an abstract base a consumer derives from, such as an abstract handler base declared beside the contract it serves.
      • extension(Type type) (line 49): SimpleName (line 56) strips the generic-arity backtick so suffix conventions match generic types too. InheritsGeneric (line 67) walks the base chain and ImplementsGeneric (line 81) scans the interface set for an open generic. HasBaseTypeStartingWith (line 89) detects a framework base by full-name prefix without a compile dependency (for example FluentValidation's AbstractValidator). DeclaredPublicProperties (line 103) narrows to declared-only public instance properties. InheritsAggregateRoot (line 110) and InheritsAuditableEntity (line 117) hard-code the MMCA entity base full names (AuditableAggregateRootEntity<TIdentifierType> plus the AuditableBaseEntity<TIdentifierType> and BaseEntity<TIdentifierType> ancestors) so the entity rules can classify types cross-repo.
      • extension(PropertyInfo property) (line 123): HasPublicMutableSetter (line 130) is the immutability primitive. It reports false when there is no public setter, and false for init-only setters by looking for the System.Runtime.CompilerServices.IsExternalInit required custom modifier on the setter's return parameter (lines 140-144).
    • Why it's built this way: every helper avoids a compile-time reference to the type it detects (base types matched by string prefix), which is what lets one rule body run identically across four repos that do not reference each other. The class carries a file-level [SuppressMessage] for CA1708 (lines 10-13): with multiple extension(T) blocks in one static class the analyzer flags the compiler-generated grouping members as case-colliding, a documented false positive.
    • Where it's used: throughout the ArchitectureRules partials, inside CrossEntityNavigationFinder, and directly by RouteAuthorizationTestsBase and AnonymousEndpointTestsBase.
    • Caveats / not-in-source: the type is internal, so consumer repos cannot call these helpers directly; they reach the same behavior only through the public rules and bases. StateManagementConventionTestsBase is the one base that re-implements the tolerant type load privately rather than using this class (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture/Bases/Ui/StateManagementConventionTestsBase.cs:142).

    ArchitectureAssert

    MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture · MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture · MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture/ArchitectureAssert.cs:8 · Level 1 · static class

    • What it is: the shared failure-reporting helper for every architecture fitness function, a static class with two NoViolations overloads that turn a rule breach into a readable, offender-listing assertion failure.
    • Depends on: ArchitectureRuleResult, the result type of the package's own dependency rules (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture/ArchitectureRuleResult.cs:4), and AwesomeAssertions' Should() fluent API, global-imported for the whole package (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture/GlobalUsings.cs:3). It has no other first-party dependency: this is the bottom of the fitness-function stack.
    • Concept introduced, architecture fitness functions. A fitness function is an automated test that asserts a structural property of the codebase (a layer never references another, a controller is sealed) rather than a behavioral one. This package makes those rules first-class, shared code (ADR-015). [Rubric §14, Testability] assesses how well invariants are guarded by executable checks; ArchitectureAssert is the reporting primitive that makes a failing invariant name its offenders instead of just going red. [Rubric §34, Architecture Governance] assesses whether architectural decisions are enforced rather than merely documented; every rule in this package funnels its verdict through here.
    • Walkthrough
      • NoViolations(ArchitectureRuleResult result, string reason) (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture/ArchitectureAssert.cs:11) null-guards the result (line 13), joins FailingTypeNames into a bullet list (line 15), and asserts IsSuccessful.Should().BeTrue(...) with the reason plus the violation list as the because argument (lines 17-18).
      • NoViolations(IEnumerable<string> violations, string reason) (line 22) materializes the sequence once and asserts list.Should().BeEmpty(...) (line 26), for the reflection-derived, IL-reading and file-scanning rules that produce a plain string list rather than an ArchitectureRuleResult.
    • Why it's built this way: the XML doc (lines 3-7) splits the two overloads by the kind of rule they serve: one reports an ArchitectureRuleResult from the dependency rules (ArchitectureTypes), the other a reflection- or IL-derived violation list. Every rule, whatever its engine, therefore fails in the same format, the reason followed by the offender list (the first overload bullets each failing type name itself, line 15), and no repo carries its own copy of that reporting logic.
    • Where it's used: every rule in ArchitectureRules and several reflection-based test bases call one of these two overloads as their final step.

    TypeSig

    MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture · MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture.Metadata · MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture/Metadata/TypeSig.cs:52 · Level 1 · internal sealed class

    • What it is: the read-only type model the metadata-reading architecture rules reason over: one type as a signature, a base-type slot or an IL operand names it (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture/Metadata/TypeSig.cs:39-51).
    • Depends on: TypeSigKind; from System.Reflection.Metadata, TypeDefinitionHandle, PrimitiveTypeCode, ArrayShape and MethodSignature<T>; System.Collections.Immutable for its argument and dimension arrays.
    • Concept introduced, a type model read from metadata, not from loaded types. The dependency and IL rules read compiled assemblies through System.Reflection.Metadata: the decoder SignatureProvider implements ISignatureTypeProvider<TypeSig, GenericScope> (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture/Metadata/SignatureProvider.cs:20), so every type a signature, base-type slot or IL operand names becomes a TypeSig without loading the type. Names follow the ECMA-335 metadata spelling rather than the reflection one: a nested type reads Namespace.Outer/Inner, a generic type keeps its arity marker (List`1), a closed generic lists its arguments in angle brackets, and a modified type carries its modifier as a suffix (lines 40-45). A wrapper (array, pointer, reference, pinned or modified type) reports the namespace of what it wraps and that type's name plus its own suffix and is never nested; a generic instance reports the name, namespace and declaring type of its definition (lines 46-49). [Rubric §34, Architecture Governance] assesses whether architectural decisions are enforced by executable checks; this model is what the dependency rules' verdicts are computed over, so its spelling is the contract every forbidden-dependency name is written against.
    • Walkthrough
      • State: the private constructor (line 58) takes kind, name, namespace, declaring type and a wrapper suffix; the static PrimitiveNames table (line 54) is built once by BuildPrimitiveNames (line 203), indexed by PrimitiveTypeCode.
      • Properties: Kind (line 68), Name (line 71), Namespace (line 74), DeclaringType (line 77) with IsNested derived from it (line 80); Definition (line 86), the definition handle inside the producing module, nil for a type defined elsewhere and for every shape other than Named; Element (line 89), Arguments (line 92), Dimensions (line 95) and ReturnType (line 98) for the wrapping, generic and function-pointer shapes. FullName (line 101) is computed once and cached through the C# field keyword, and ElementType (line 104) recurses to the innermost wrapped type.
      • Factories: CreateNamed (line 107), CreatePrimitive (line 111, a System named type from the table), CreateGenericInstance (line 115, copies the definition's name, namespace and declaring type and keeps the definition as Element), CreateVector (line 123, suffix []), CreateArray (line 126, per-dimension bounds from the ArrayShape, upper bound computed as lower plus size minus one, lines 131-132), CreatePointer (line 145, *), CreateByReference (line 148, &), CreatePinned (line 151, no suffix), CreateModified (line 154, modreq(...) or modopt(...)), CreateGenericParameter (line 158, positional !0 or !!0 when the owner's name is unknown, lines 160-161) and CreateFunctionPointer (line 166). Every wrapper goes through the private Wrap (line 173).
      • Spelling: ArraySuffix (line 176) prints [] for one unbounded dimension and [lo...hi,...] otherwise. BuildFullName (line 227) qualifies a named type by namespace and joins a nested one to its declaring type with / (lines 231-232), appends <args> to a generic instance's definition (line 237), prints a function pointer as method R *(args) (line 242), and otherwise appends the wrapper suffix to the element's full name (line 245).
    • Why it's built this way: the constructor is private, so every instance comes from a named factory that fixes the shape's spelling, and FullName is cached because consumers key on it repeatedly: DependencyNameTree caches each match by (Kind, FullName) (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture/Metadata/DependencyNameTree.cs:62).
    • Where it's used: produced by SignatureProvider and MetadataModule, held by MetadataType, MetadataMethod and MetadataMethodBody (Locals), carried in IL operands (MethodOperand, FieldOperand), matched by DependencyNameTree and TypeDependencyScan, and read by CallGraphIndex and the domain-event-handler-saves and cascade soft-delete rules.
    • Caveats / not-in-source: internal, so consumer repos never see it.

    DependencyNameTree

    MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture · MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture.Metadata · MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture/Metadata/DependencyNameTree.cs:20 · Level 2 · internal sealed class

    • What it is: the set of dependency names a rule looks for (namespaces or type full names), held as a tree of name segments so a type is matched in one walk (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture/Metadata/DependencyNameTree.cs:6-19).
    • Depends on: TypeSig, TypeSigKind; System.Buffers.SearchValues<char> for the separator scans and NormalizationForm for Unicode normalization.
    • Concept introduced, segment-prefix matching. A name matches a type when its segments are a leading run of the type's own segments: the namespace (for a nested type, the declaring type's full name) followed by the type name. Segments split on ., :, / and + and compare whole and ordinally (lines 7-11). The doc spells out the consequences (lines 12-18): Azure matches Azure.Messaging.ServiceBus and every type in it; MMCA.Common.AI never matches MMCA.Common.API, because AI and API are different segments; an entry ending in a dot matches nothing; a generic type matches through its arity marker, and its type arguments are matched separately. [Rubric §34, Architecture Governance] applies: this is the matching core behind the layer and module isolation rules, and whole-segment comparison is what keeps a namespace rule from catching a sibling namespace that merely shares a prefix.
    • Walkthrough
      • Fields: the Separators (line 22) and Unsupported (line 23) character sets, the _root node (line 25), and the _matches cache keyed by (Kind, FullName) (line 26).
      • The constructor (line 30) rejects any name containing ,, [, ], *, & or \ with an ArgumentException (assembly qualifiers, generic argument lists and array, pointer or reference suffixes are not supported, lines 35-40), inserts each name's segments, and counts distinct names in TerminatedCount (lines 48-52, property at line 57).
      • Match(TypeSig) (line 60) returns the tree nodes a type matches, walking its tokens once per distinct type and caching the result (lines 62-67). MatchesAny(string) (line 73) walks a single full name.
      • Segments (line 76) keeps an empty segment wherever two separators touch or the name ends in one, which is why a trailing-dot entry can never terminate on a real segment.
      • Tokens/AddTokens (lines 97, 104) build the type's pieces in reading order: an array, pointer or reference emits its element's tokens then a suffix token from SuffixToken (lines 106-110, helper at line 135); otherwise the namespace or declaring type and the name (lines 113-119); a generic instance then appends < and each argument's tokens followed by , (lines 127-132).
      • Walk (line 150) descends segment by segment, yields every terminated node it passes, and stops at the first segment no name continues into (lines 157-165).
      • The nested Node (line 170) holds ordinally compared children (line 172) and normalizes every segment to Unicode form C on insert and on lookup (lines 178, 189).
    • Why it's built this way: the Tokens doc (lines 89-96) states the design: only the leading pieces can match a supported name, and the trailing markers keep a walk from matching across a boundary it should not; the list is built eagerly because Match caches the walk per distinct type, and the walk still stops at the first piece no name continues into.
    • Where it's used: ArchitectureTypes holds a static tree of excluded namespaces (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture/ArchitectureTypes.cs:39) and builds one per dependency rule call (lines 112, 164, 173); TypeDependencyScan.DependsOnAny and DependsOnAll take one (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture/Metadata/TypeDependencyScan.cs:39, :43).

An IlInstruction carries an operand that is a MethodOperand, a FieldOperand, a TypeSig for a type token, the literal of an ldstr, or null for every other kind (branch targets, numbers, locals and arguments, calli signatures), "none of which a rule reads" (lines 8-12). Resolving the metadata token into a typed record up front lets an IL rule pattern-match on what an instruction touches instead of decoding tokens itself.

    MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture · MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture · MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture/IArchitectureMap.cs:39 · Level 2 · interface

    • What it is: the single per-repo abstraction every architecture fitness function keys off. Each repo supplies one implementation declaring its layer and module assemblies; the shared rule library and abstract test bases consume only this interface, so a rule is written once and runs identically across every repo that supplies a map (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture/IArchitectureMap.cs:33-38, whose doc names MMCA.Common, MMCA.Store and MMCA.ADC; MMCA.Helpdesk supplies a fourth map).
    • Depends on: LayerRef, Layer, System.Reflection.Assembly.
    • Concept introduced, the architecture map as the fitness-function extension point. This is a classic Dependency Inversion: the rules depend on an abstraction (the map), and each repo provides the concrete inventory of its assemblies. [Rubric §1, SOLID] (DIP) and [Rubric §7, Microservices Readiness] apply: the map also models the per-module layers a would-be extracted service owns, so the isolation rules can check module boundaries the same way in any repo.
    • Walkthrough: the interface exposes identity (RepoToken line 42, ModuleNames line 45), the raw Layers inventory (line 48), and the projections the rules lean on: OfLayer (all assemblies of a kind, line 51), the per-module ModuleDomain/ModuleApplication/ModuleShared (lines 54-60), Infrastructure()/Api() across framework plus modules (lines 63-66), the lookups For(module, layer) (line 69) and ModuleOf(assembly) (line 72), namespace derivation RootNamespace(module, layer) (line 75), and OtherModuleNamespaces (line 81), which returns the same-layer namespaces of every other module (the forbidden targets for a module-isolation rule, empty for framework layers and single-module repos).
    • Why it's built this way: funneling every rule through one interface is what removed the drifting per-repo copies of the architecture-test suite (ADR-015); add a repo and you write one map, not a new rule set.
    • Where it's used: held as the protected abstract IArchitectureMap Map on nearly every *TestsBase in this group and passed to nearly every method of ArchitectureRules. ArchitectureMapBase is the reusable partial implementation, and CommonArchitectureMap / AdcArchitectureMap are two of the four concrete maps (Store and Helpdesk supply the others).

    SpanishAccentTestsBase

    MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture · MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture · MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture/Bases/Governance/SpanishAccentTestsBase.cs:28 · Level 2 · abstract class

    • What it is: a localization-quality fitness function: no *.es.resx file under a repo's resource root may carry a common Spanish word with its accent or n-tilde missing (for example the unaccented sesion or contrasena spellings of the words that need an accent or an n-tilde), so a new Spanish UI string cannot silently regress.
    • Depends on: ArchitectureAssert (NoViolations, line 124), ArchitectureMapBase.FindRepoRoot (only in the subclass, to build the root), System.Xml.Linq (XDocument), System.Text.RegularExpressions, AwesomeAssertions.
    • Concept introduced, a text-quality gate over resource files. Like FormsConventionTestsBase it reads files rather than assemblies, but here the subject is translated UI text. A word list of unaccented spellings (DefaultUnaccentedWords, MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture/Bases/Governance/SpanishAccentTestsBase.cs:34-41, 33 words including sesion, codigo, contrasena, numero, pagina, aqui, mas) is compiled into one case-insensitive whole-word regex with a one-second match timeout (lines 84-88), and every data/value pair in every *.es.resx is matched against it. Words that are correct both with and without the accent depending on meaning are deliberately left off the list: the class doc names esta, solo and aun ("even" unaccented, "still" accented), and it also leaves out the first-person verb forms UI text uses unaccented (confirmo in "Confirmo que acepto...", visito) (lines 20-25).
    • Walkthrough: the subclass supplies one abstract member and may override three virtual ones.
      • ResourceRoot (line 47) is the folder scanned recursively, normally the repo's Source folder under ArchitectureMapBase.FindRepoRoot("<Repo>.slnx").
      • UnaccentedWords (line 53) defaults to the framework list; a subclass extends it with [.. base.UnaccentedWords, "extra"] for domain vocabulary.
      • AllowedEntries (line 60, default empty) lists intentional exceptions as {path relative to the root, forward slashes}:{resource key}, exactly as a failure prints them; the doc comment frames an exception as a decision, not a way to make the gate pass.
      • MinimumResourceFileCount (line 66, default 1) is the anti-vacuity floor: a wrong root that finds no *.es.resx fails instead of passing with nothing checked (lines 80-82).
      • The single [Fact] Spanish_resources_keep_their_accents (lines 68-69) asserts the root is set and exists (lines 71-72), enumerates and ordinally sorts the files while skipping build output through IsBuildOutput (lines 74-78, helper at line 131: any path segment bin, obj, node_modules or .git), skips non-string entries that carry a type or mimetype attribute (lines 100-103) and any AllowedEntries hit (lines 108-111), and collects file:key: words offenders reported through ArchitectureAssert.NoViolations (lines 119, 124-127).
    • Why it's built this way: the offender line is formatted to be pasted straight into AllowedEntries, so the fix path (correct the value, or record the exception) is in the failure itself. Keeping the word list short and the matcher whole-word keeps false positives rare enough that exceptions stay exceptional.
    • Where it's used: subclassed with only ResourceRoot overridden in MMCA.Common (MMCA.Common/Tests/Architecture/MMCA.Common.Architecture.Tests/Governance/SpanishAccentTests.cs:11, root at :13-14, so the framework's own UI strings are held to the rule every consumer inherits), in ADC (MMCA.ADC/Tests/Architecture/MMCA.ADC.Architecture.Tests/Governance/SpanishAccentTests.cs:10, root at :12-13) and in Store (MMCA.Store/Tests/Architecture/MMCA.Store.Architecture.Tests/Governance/SpanishAccentTests.cs:8, root at :10-11). MMCA.Common also pins the base's own behavior against fixture resources in SpanishAccentFitnessTests (MMCA.Common/Tests/Architecture/MMCA.Common.Architecture.Tests/Governance/Localization/SpanishAccentFitnessTests.cs:12), through a private subclass that points ResourceRoot at a fixture tree (:47-49).

    ConstructorDependencyCountTestsBase

    MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture · MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture · MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture/Bases/Cqrs/ConstructorDependencyCountTestsBase.cs:29 · Level 3 · abstract class

    • What it is: a single-responsibility-ceiling fitness function applied to three injection points a module composes: Application-layer *Service facades, API controllers, and CQRS command/query handlers. It fails the build if any concrete class in a population has a constructor with more than that population's accepted dependency count.
    • Depends on: IArchitectureMap (via Map.ModuleApplication() and Map.Api() in the default populations), [Fact], AwesomeAssertions, and reflection over constructors (System.Reflection.ConstructorInfo) and interfaces.
    • Concept introduced, quantifying the SRP smell across three populations. [Rubric §1, SOLID] assesses single-responsibility discipline; a ballooning constructor-dependency list is the canonical smell wherever it appears, and this base turns a previously implicit judgement call into an enforced, per-population ceiling so the next class cannot silently grow past it (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture/Bases/Cqrs/ConstructorDependencyCountTestsBase.cs:5-28). Each ceiling is a ratchet, not a budget: a consumer sets it at its current high-water mark, raises it only as a recorded deliberate decision, and lowers it the moment remediation makes a lower number true (lines 14-19, enforced in both directions by the *_DoNotExceedConstructorDependencyCeiling and *_ConstructorDependencyCeilingIsTight facts). What gets measured is itself an extension point: the three populations and the constructors measured on each type are virtual, with defaults that reproduce the module scan, so a consumer that overrides nothing scans exactly the module populations (lines 22-26).
    • Walkthrough: the subclass supplies Map (line 37), plus one abstract ceiling per population: MaxConstructorDependencies for Application services (line 43), MaxControllerConstructorDependencies for API controllers (line 50), and MaxHandlerConstructorDependencies for CQRS handlers (line 58). Four virtual members say what is measured:
      • ScannedServices (line 64) defaults to every concrete class whose name ends in Service in Map.ModuleApplication() (lines 65-68).
      • ScannedControllers (line 74) and ScannedHandlers (line 81) default to the shared private Scan (line 240, flat-maps ConcreteClasses, excludes nested and compiler-generated types) over Map.Api() and Map.ModuleApplication(), filtered by IsController (line 259, matches the full name Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.ControllerBase via HasBaseTypeStartingWith) or IsCommandOrQueryHandler (line 262, matches a generic interface whose definition's full name starts with the ICommandHandler/IQueryHandler prefix constants, lines 34-35).
      • MeasuredConstructors(Type) (line 89) defaults to type.GetConstructors(), the public instance constructors (line 92); the widest measured constructor is the type's dependency count, computed by the private WidestConstructor (line 230).
      • Three ceiling facts share one shape: materialize the population, assert non-vacuity, assert no offender. ApplicationServices_DoNotExceedConstructorDependencyCeiling (line 96), Controllers_DoNotExceedConstructorDependencyCeiling (line 119) and Handlers_DoNotExceedConstructorDependencyCeiling (line 143) each assert non-vacuity first (lines 100-101, 123-124, 147-148) and report offenders by name and count through the shared instance helper Offenders (line 248), which measures each type with WidestConstructor (line 253) and so honors the overridable MeasuredConstructors.
      • Three tightness facts enforce the other direction of the ratchet: ApplicationServices_ConstructorDependencyCeilingIsTight (line 168), Controllers_ConstructorDependencyCeilingIsTight (line 181) and Handlers_ConstructorDependencyCeilingIsTight (line 194) each delegate to the private AssertCeilingIsTight (line 207). It asserts the population is non-empty, finds the observed maximum and the classes sitting at it, and fails when the declared ceiling exceeds that maximum; the message names the population, the ceiling property, its value, the observed maximum and the widest classes, so the fix (lower the ceiling to the observed number) is in the failure itself.
      • Controller and handler matching is by full type-name string, not a compiled reference to Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc or MMCA.Common.Application, so the rule library keeps zero compile dependency on either (lines 31-35).
    • Why it's built this way: splitting the ceiling by population lets each stay honest: a controller is a thin translation layer over handlers, so a long injection list there means it serves more than one resource, while a handler serves exactly one use case and is the population where a long list is least defensible (lines 112-117, 136-141). The tightness facts exist because a ceiling left above the observed maximum is a budget, not a ratchet: the next class can grow into the slack without anything failing (lines 161-166). It overlaps the arity check in HandlerConventionTestsBase but scopes specifically to these three facades and lets a repo pin an exact number per population rather than take a shared default. Making the populations and the measured constructors virtual is what lets a repo without business modules adopt the same gate: per the summary doc, MMCA.Common overrides them to scan its framework assemblies (lines 22-23).
    • Where it's used: MMCA.Common subclasses it over its own framework in FrameworkConstructorDependencyTests (MMCA.Common/Tests/Architecture/MMCA.Common.Architecture.Tests/Cqrs/ConstructorDependencies/FrameworkConstructorDependencyTests.cs:25): the populations are every top-level class in the Application and Infrastructure assemblies, ControllerBase-derived classes in the API assembly, and handler implementations in the Application assembly, abstract classes included (:42-49), and MeasuredConstructors widens to public and protected constructors because the widest framework classes are abstract bases whose only constructors are protected (:51-53, rationale :8-12). Its ceilings are 7 for services (:33), 5 for controllers (:37, held by CrudEntityControllerBase, InboxController and UserAccountAuthControllerBase) and 7 for handlers (:40, held by ResetPasswordHandlerBase). The base's own behavior is pinned by ConstructorDependencyCountTestsBaseTests. It is also subclassed in ADC (MMCA.ADC/Tests/Architecture/MMCA.ADC.Architecture.Tests/Cqrs/ConstructorDependencyCountTests.cs:20) with MaxConstructorDependencies at 9 (:24, held by AuthenticationService, history at :9-18), MaxControllerConstructorDependencies at 10 (:52, held by SessionsController, history at :26-51), and MaxHandlerConstructorDependencies at 7 (:61, held jointly by ResetPasswordHandler and SubmitQuestionHandler, rationale at :54-60). Store subclasses it with a service ceiling of 8, one below ADC because Store is local-credential only and has no external-login email verifier (MMCA.Store/Tests/Architecture/MMCA.Store.Architecture.Tests/Cqrs/ConstructorDependencyCountTests.cs:26, ceiling at :24, rationale at :8-18). MMCA.Helpdesk deliberately does not adopt it and records why in a comment: its Application layer is handlers-only, and the base's anti-vacuity guard fails when it finds no *Service at all (MMCA.Helpdesk/Tests/Architecture/MMCA.Helpdesk.Architecture.Tests/ArchitectureTests.cs:177-179).

    IlReader

    MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture · MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture.Metadata · MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture/Metadata/IlReader.cs:52 · Level 3 · internal static class

    • What it is: the decoder that turns a method body's raw IL byte stream into a list of instructions, each carrying its opcode and, for the operand kinds a rule reads, a resolved operand: a method, a field, a type, or the literal of an ldstr.
    • Depends on: MetadataModule (operand resolution), the sibling IlInstruction, MethodOperand and FieldOperand declared in the same file (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture/Metadata/IlReader.cs:13, :34, :49), and the BCL System.Reflection.Emit.OpCodes and System.Reflection.Metadata.BlobReader (lines 2-4).
    • Concept introduced, reading IL without a third-party library. The opcode set is not hand-written: the static constructor (line 57) reflects over every public static OpCode field of System.Reflection.Emit.OpCodes and files each one into a 256-slot table by its value, one table for single-byte opcodes and one for the 0xFE-prefixed two-byte opcodes (lines 54-55, 59-75). Decoding is then a table lookup per instruction. [Rubric §32, Dependency & Supply-Chain] assesses how much third-party code a package pulls in; this decoder keeps the body-reading rules on the BCL alone (the using list at lines 1-4 is the whole external surface).
    • Walkthrough
      • Read(module, il, scope) (line 79) loops while bytes remain (lines 84-91): it reads an opcode, reads its operand, links the new instruction to the previous one through IlInstruction.Follow (line 88, so a rule can look one instruction back, for example at a constrained. prefix), and returns the list.
      • ReadOpCode (line 96) picks the two-byte table when the first byte is 0xFE (line 99) and throws InvalidOperationException naming the byte for an opcode neither table knows (line 100).
      • ReadOperand (line 103) resolves only what a rule reads: InlineString to the user string (lines 107-110), InlineMethod through MetadataModule.ResolveMethod (lines 112-115), InlineField through ResolveField (lines 117-120), InlineType through DecodeType (lines 122-125), InlineTok through ResolveToken (lines 127-130). A switch skips its jump table (lines 132-137); every other operand is skipped by size (line 139) and yields a null operand.
      • ResolveToken (line 144) decides whether an ldtoken names a method (a method definition or specification, or a member reference whose kind is method), a field, or a type.
      • SkippedOperandSize (line 160) returns 0, 1, 2, 8 or 4 bytes by operand type (lines 162-177).
    • Why it's built this way: the rules that look inside bodies (handler saves, clock reads, domain throws, cascade soft delete) need calls, field touches, type tokens and string literals, nothing else, so branch targets, numbers, locals and calli signatures are skipped rather than modelled (doc, lines 9-11 and 159).
    • Where it's used: only by MetadataMethod, whose lazy body read calls IlReader.Read (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture/Metadata/MetadataMethod.cs:142).
    • Caveats / not-in-source: internal, so a consumer reaches it only through the public rules.

      • The constructor (line 17) reads the name, the metadata token (line 28, the same number reflection's MemberInfo.MetadataToken reports, which is how MetadataModule.FindMethod(int) maps a reflected method back), and the Static, Virtual and Abstract flags (lines 30-32).

    MetadataModule

    MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture · MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture.Metadata · MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture/Metadata/MetadataModule.cs:25 · Level 3 · internal sealed class

    • What it is: one compiled assembly read straight from its file through System.Reflection.Metadata, with nothing loaded into the runtime: every type definition (nested ones included), each type's members and signatures, and each method body's IL on demand. It is the single reader behind the dependency rules and the rules that look inside method bodies (doc, MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture/Metadata/MetadataModule.cs:10-14).
    • Depends on: MetadataType, MetadataMethod, MetadataAttribute, SignatureProvider, and the BCL System.Reflection.Metadata and System.Reflection.PortableExecutable.PEReader (lines 1-6). No third-party package.
    • Concept introduced, a metadata-only assembly model. Architecture rules need two things reflection is poor at: the contents of method bodies, and reading an assembly without loading it (and its dependencies) into the test process. This type reads the PE file's metadata tables directly and builds an immutable object model over them. [Rubric §14, Testability] assesses whether invariants can be checked mechanically; this model is what lets the package check invariants that live inside method bodies. [Rubric §32, Dependency & Supply-Chain] applies because the reader is the BCL plus this package's own code. The module is read once per file for the life of the process: the file is copied into managed memory, so no file handle stays open, and every member is immutable once built, so rules running in parallel share it (doc, lines 15-19; the CA1001 suppression at lines 21-24 records why the PEReader is never disposed).
    • Walkthrough
      • State: a process-wide Cache of Lazy<MetadataModule> keyed by full path, case-insensitively (line 27); the PEReader (line 29); signature caches per definition, reference and primitive (lines 30-32); and the method-by-handle map (line 33).
      • The private constructor (line 35) wraps the bytes in a PEReader (line 37), binds a SignatureProvider (line 39), reads the assembly name (line 40), then builds every top-level type and, depth-first through AddWithNested (line 223), its nested types (lines 43-49). Types (line 61) keeps that order and includes the <Module> pseudo-type (doc, lines 57-60).
      • Load(path) (line 71) is the only entry point: it normalizes the path and returns the cached read, constructing it at most once per path through GetOrAdd plus Lazy (line 76).
      • Lookup: FindMethod(int metadataToken) (line 80) and FindMethod(MethodDefinitionHandle) (line 87) over the map that each MetadataMethod fills through Register (line 90).
      • Signatures: Primitive (line 93), DefinitionSig (line 96) and ReferenceSig (line 109) build and cache TypeSig nodes, nesting through the declaring type; DecodeType (line 120) handles TypeDef, TypeRef and TypeSpec handles and throws for anything else (line 137).
      • Attributes (line 145) and Constraints (line 149) build the attribute and generic-constraint arrays every member type uses.
      • Operands for IlReader: ResolveMethod (line 157) covers method definitions, member references (through MemberParent) and method specifications, the last carrying the decoded generic arguments (lines 173-178); ResolveField (line 184) covers field definitions and member references.
      • LeadingStringArgument (line 202) reads a custom attribute blob: it requires the 0x0001 prolog (line 205) and returns the first serialized string, or null when the first argument is not a string or type.
      • GetMethodBody (line 221) hands an RVA to the PEReader. The private MemberParent (line 240) returns a member reference's declaring type, its definition when it is local, and the generic scope its signature is read in; a type defined elsewhere gets GenericScope.None (lines 248-251), and an unrecognized parent falls back to <Module> (line 266).
    • Why it's built this way: reading by name from metadata keeps the package free of compile references to the code it governs and free of an IL library dependency, while the per-path cache means a whole architecture test run reads each assembly once however many rules scan it.
    • Where it's used: every rule that needs metadata loads through Load: the dependency engine (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture/ArchitectureTypes.cs:63), the error-catalog, clock-read, domain-throws, soft-delete and substitutability rules (Rules/Contracts/ArchitectureRules.ErrorCatalog.cs:170, Rules/Domain/ArchitectureRules.ClockReads.cs:81, Rules/Domain/ArchitectureRules.DomainThrows.cs:83, Rules/Domain/ArchitectureRules.SoftDelete.cs:73, Rules/Governance/ArchitectureRules.Substitutability.cs:61, all under MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture/), and the three call-graph rules that feed CallGraphIndex.
    • Caveats / not-in-source: internal; the cache is never evicted, by design (doc, lines 16-19).

    CallGraphIndex

    MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture · MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture · MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture/CallGraphIndex.cs:20 · Level 4 · internal sealed class

    • What it is: a read-only index over the compiled assemblies an IL-reading rule scans, built once per rule run. It holds every type by full name, every type's transitive ancestor names, and the reverse map from an ancestor name to the scanned types that implement or derive from it.
    • Depends on: the package's own metadata layer: MetadataModule (the constructor input), MetadataType, MetadataMethod, and the TypeSig and MethodOperand models, all read through the BCL System.Reflection.Metadata; plus BCL dictionaries and HashSet<string>. No third-party package.
    • Concept introduced, following an interface call in a static walk. IL records the static callee: a handler that calls IPointsAwarder.AwardAsync emits a callvirt naming the interface method, not the class that does the work. A walk that stops there never reaches the implementation, so a transitive rule would report nothing. The reverse implementor map is what closes that gap (doc, lines 9-13). The second design decision is equally load-bearing: ancestors are recorded by name, not by resolved definition, so a contract declared in an assembly the map does not register (typically a framework interface such as IDomainEventHandler<T>) is still recognized as an ancestor; only the walk through such a type stops, because its metadata is absent (doc, lines 14-18). [Rubric §14, Testability] assesses whether behavioral invariants inside method bodies can be checked at all; this index is the primitive that makes the body-reading rules in this package possible without a Roslyn or IL-rewriting dependency.
    • Walkthrough
      • Three ordinal-keyed dictionaries back the index: _types by full name, _ancestors per type, and _implementors from an ancestor name to the derived types (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture/CallGraphIndex.cs:22-24).
      • The constructor (line 26) makes two passes: it registers every type in every module, nested types included (lines 28-31), then computes each type's ancestor set and inverts it into _implementors (lines 33-48).
      • Types (line 52) exposes the whole inventory. ElementFullName (line 55) strips a generic instantiation down to the open definition's name, which is how a reference to a closed generic still matches the type it was declared as.
      • Implements(type, ancestorFullName) (line 58) is the membership test the handler and cascade rules select on. Find(TypeSig?) (line 63) resolves a reference to a scanned type or null when it lives outside the scan, and the Find(string) overload (line 67) does the same for a full metadata name.
      • TargetsOf(MethodOperand callee) (line 75) is the core: it resolves the declaring type (returning nothing when it is outside the scan, lines 77-81), collects the directly matching methods (line 83), and returns them unchanged when the declaring type is not an interface and no direct match is virtual or abstract (lines 84-87); otherwise it adds every matching method on every known implementor (lines 89-90). Overload resolution is approximated by name and parameter count, which deliberately over-approximates so no real path is missed (doc, lines 69-74).
      • MatchingMethods (line 97) requires a body and an equal ParameterTypes length, and accepts either an exact name match or a .-suffix match, because an explicit interface implementation is named Some.Ns.IFoo.Method in metadata (doc, lines 93-96).
      • ComputeAncestors (line 119) walks base types and interfaces with an explicit stack, adding each name once and descending only into definitions the scan actually contains (lines 125-141), which is both cycle-safe and tolerant of out-of-scan contracts.
    • Why it's built this way: the package's whole stance is zero compile references to the code it governs (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture.csproj:22-29), and reading assembly metadata by name through MetadataModule is the same discipline applied one level deeper. Building the index once per rule run, rather than resolving references per call site, is what keeps a transitive breadth-first walk over a whole repo's assemblies fast enough to sit in a normal test run.
    • Where it's used: by the three IL-walking rules that need to follow calls rather than just find them, each building one index from MetadataModule.Load over the scanned assemblies: the cascade soft-delete rule (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture/Rules/Domain/ArchitectureRules.CascadeSoftDelete.cs:107), the domain-event-handler save rule (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture/Rules/Cqrs/ArchitectureRules.DomainEventHandlerSaves.cs:85), and the query-handler repository rule over the Application assemblies (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture/Rules/Cqrs/ArchitectureRules.QueryHandlerRepositories.cs:44). The first two surface through CascadeSoftDeleteConventionTestsBase and DomainEventHandlerSaveTestsBase.
    • Caveats / not-in-source: the type is internal, so a consumer repo cannot build its own call-graph rule on top of it; the reach is only through the public rules.

So westus does not match "West US 2" and centralus does not match "South Central US" (lines 47-53), which keeps a forbidden region that is a prefix of the real one from failing the gate, and a stated region that is only a prefix of another from passing it.

    RawQueryableConventionTestsBase

    MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture · MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture · MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture/Bases/Cqrs/RawQueryableConventionTestsBase.cs:31 · Level 4 · abstract partial class

    • What it is: an opt-in extraction-readiness gate: Application-layer code must not use the repository's raw IQueryable surfaces (Table, TableNoTracking, TableNoTrackingSingleQuery, TableNoTrackingSplitQuery on IReadRepository<TEntity, TIdentifierType>), because a handler written against a raw queryable is EF-coupled and its query shape cannot cross a gRPC boundary.
    • Depends on: IArchitectureMap, ArchitectureMapBase.FindRepoRoot, ArchitectureAssert, System.IO enumeration, and a source-generated Regex (System.Text.RegularExpressions).
    • Concept introduced, the honest textual scan (and its stated limits). The doc is unusually candid about the tradeoff (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture/Bases/Cqrs/RawQueryableConventionTestsBase.cs:13-24): plain reflection cannot see member usage inside method bodies, the package deliberately carries no Roslyn dependency, and this rule does not use the IL reader the call-graph rules use, so the rule reads .cs text instead. It cannot see through variable indirection (an interface alias re-exposing the queryable is missed), and because it skips only whole-line comments, a match inside a string literal or trailing comment is a rare false positive. [Rubric §7, Microservices Readiness] is the invariant being protected; [Rubric §8, Data Architecture] and [Rubric §15, Best Practices & Code Quality] apply to the handler style it pushes toward (focused repository methods, readers, queriers, specifications).
    • Walkthrough
      • AllowedFiles (line 38) is the adoption ratchet: a repo with existing violations subclasses, runs once, and moves the reported file names in, so new files stay clean while the list shrinks (lines 24-28).
      • ApplicationSourceDirectories() (line 45) defaults to locating each declared module's Application project directory under the repo's Source/ tree by project name (lines 47-57), and is virtual for a custom layout.
      • The [Fact] ApplicationLayer_DoesNotUseRawQueryableSurfaces (line 61) first asserts the directory list is non-empty, with a message telling the author to override the directory hook (lines 65-66), then enumerates every .cs file, skipping obj, bin, and allowlisted file names (lines 71-79), and reports through ArchitectureAssert.NoViolations (line 84).
      • ScanFile (line 88) yields a file-name, line-number and trimmed-line triple for every non-comment line matching RawQueryableAccessRegex (line 103), a [GeneratedRegex] partial property matching the Table and TableNoTracking member-access family with a 2000 ms match timeout.
    • Why it's built this way: making the offender message carry the file and line (lines 96-98) is what makes a textual gate actionable; combined with the allowlist ratchet it can be adopted in a repo that is not yet clean. Note the contrast with the IL-reading rules in ArchitectureRules, which do read method bodies: a member read on a property is what a text scan is cheapest at, while a call is what Cecil sees best.
    • Where it's used: subclassed opt-in in MMCA.Common (MMCA.Common/Tests/Architecture/MMCA.Common.Architecture.Tests/Cqrs/RawQueryableConventionTests.cs:13), Store (MMCA.Store/Tests/Architecture/MMCA.Store.Architecture.Tests/Cqrs/RawQueryableConventionTests.cs:9), and ADC (MMCA.ADC/Tests/Architecture/MMCA.ADC.Architecture.Tests/Cqrs/RawQueryableConventionTests.cs:11). Because it is a ratchet, a repo's AllowedFiles override is the record of its remaining debt.

      • The private GetLoadableTypes (line 142) repeats the tolerant load locally rather than using the internal RuleHelpers, and IsCompilerGenerated (line 154) treats any member name containing an angle bracket as generated, or one carrying CompilerGeneratedAttribute.
    • Where it's used: subclassed in the repos with Blazor UI assemblies: MMCA.Common (MMCA.Common/Tests/Architecture/MMCA.Common.Architecture.Tests/Ui/StateManagementConventionTests.cs:11), Store (MMCA.Store/Tests/Architecture/MMCA.Store.Architecture.Tests/Ui/StateManagementConventionTests.cs:10), and ADC (MMCA.ADC/Tests/Architecture/MMCA.ADC.Architecture.Tests/Ui/StateManagementConventionTests.cs:9).

    TypeDependencyScan

    MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture · MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture.Metadata · MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture/Metadata/TypeDependencyScan.cs:22 · Level 4 · internal sealed class

    • What it is: the dependency walker behind every "depends on" question the rule library asks: given one compiled type and a set of dependency names, it reports whether the type names at least one of them (DependsOnAny, line 39) or every one of them (DependsOnAll, line 43).
    • Depends on: the package's own metadata model (MetadataType, TypeSig, DependencyNameTree in MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture.Metadata) and System.Collections.Immutable; no reflection load and no third-party architecture library.
    • Concept introduced, a dependency is anything the compiled type names. The doc spells out the definition (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture/Metadata/TypeDependencyScan.cs:5-21): base type, interfaces, generic constraints and attribute types; field, property and event types; each method's attributes, constraints, return, parameter and local types; and every type an IL instruction names (a type token, the declaring type of a called or loaded method or field, the type arguments of a generic method instance). The compiler-generated types nested in it (lambda closures, async and iterator state machines) count as the type that wrote them. Arrays, pointers and references count as their element type, a closed generic as its definition plus each argument, and a generic parameter as nothing; a call to the type's own method or a read of its own field is not a dependency. [Rubric §34, Architecture Governance] applies: this definition is what every layer and isolation rule actually measures.
    • Walkthrough
      • Run (line 46) builds one scan holding the subject, the name tree and an enough threshold, walks the type, and returns how many distinct names it found (_found, line 27). DependsOnAny passes enough: 1; DependsOnAll passes the tree's TerminatedCount and compares the result to it.
      • CheckType (line 53) reads the type-level references, then fields, properties and events, then makes three separate passes over the methods: headers (line 84), locals (line 89), instructions (line 94), each guarded by TakeWhile(_ => !Done) (Done, line 36). The cheap signature reads therefore run first, and an Any question stops before decoding a single method body once a header has answered it. Compiler-generated nested types recurse last (line 99).
      • CheckInstructions (line 119) switches on the operand: a TypeSig token, a generic method instance (declaring type plus type arguments, line 129), and a method or field operand whose declaring definition is not the subject itself (lines 134 and 138), which is how self-calls are excluded.
      • CheckReference (line 166) skips generic parameters (line 168), unwraps array, pointer and by-ref signatures to their element (line 173), records every name the tree matches (line 183), and recurses into the arguments of a generic instance (line 188).
    • Why it's built this way: matching by name over the metadata, never by loaded Type, keeps the package free of a compile reference to anything it judges and lets a type whose dependencies cannot be resolved at run time still be inspected. The early-exit threshold keeps the per-type cost proportional to the question asked.
    • Where it's used: only through ArchitectureTypes (DoNotHaveDependencyOnAny) and ArchitectureTypeConditions (HaveDependencyOnAny, HaveDependencyOnAll), both in MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture/ArchitectureTypes.cs.

    MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture · MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture · MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture/ArchitectureTypes.cs:37 · Level 6 · sealed class

    • What it is: the package's own architecture-rule engine: the types of one compiled assembly, narrowed by predicates and then held to a dependency condition, in the shape ArchitectureTypes.InAssembly(assembly).That().HaveNameEndingWith("Controller").ShouldNot().HaveDependencyOnAny("Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore") (doc, MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture/ArchitectureTypes.cs:5-14).

The assembly is read from its file through System.Reflection.Metadata and never loaded, so a type whose dependencies cannot be resolved at run time is still inspected (lines 12-13). Dependency names match as whole dot-separated segments: Azure matches Azure and every namespace under it, MMCA.Common.AI does not match MMCA.Common.API, and an entry ending in a dot matches nothing (lines 28-31). [Rubric §3, Clean Architecture] and [Rubric §34, Architecture Governance] apply: this is the measuring instrument behind the layer and isolation rules.
    • Walkthrough
      • InAssembly (line 50) throws ArgumentException for an assembly with no file location (lines 53-58), returns an empty selection for a file that is not a .NET image (BadImageFormatException, line 65), and returns an empty selection for an assembly whose own name falls under an excluded namespace (line 70).
      • The excluded namespaces are System, Microsoft, netstandard, NuGet, Newtonsoft, xunit and Internal.Microsoft (ExcludedNamespaces, lines 39-40). IsHandWritten (line 128) also drops <Module>, <PrivateImplementationDetails>, top-level <> anonymous types and compiler-generated types, whose content counts toward the enclosing type instead (remarks, lines 17-25).
      • Predicates narrow the selection and return a new instance (Where, line 144): That() (line 77, reads as prose and changes nothing), HaveName (line 82) and HaveNameEndingWith (line 92), both case-insensitive and blind to a generic arity marker (NameWithoutArity, line 135), HaveAttribute (line 101, a declared attribute by full name, inherited ones not counted), and DoNotHaveDependencyOnAny (line 110).
      • Should() (line 118) and ShouldNot() (line 122) hand the selection to ArchitectureTypeConditions; GetTypeNames() (line 126) lists the selection in reflection spelling (Outer+Inner).
    • Why it's built this way: owning the engine keeps the dependency definition in one reviewed place (TypeDependencyScan) and lets the package match by name without referencing what it judges. ADR-015 is the fitness-function decision it serves.
    • Where it's used: the dependency rules of ArchitectureRules (ArchitectureRules.Controllers.cs, .Contracts.cs, .Ai.cs, .CloudVendors.cs, .Purity.cs, .Modules.cs), the Common-only PasswordHashingFitnessTests (MMCA.Common/Tests/Architecture/MMCA.Common.Architecture.Tests/Governance/PasswordHashingFitnessTests.cs), and its own behavior tests, ArchitectureTypesTests (MMCA.Common/Tests/Architecture/MMCA.Common.Architecture.Tests/Engine/ArchitectureTypesTests.cs, rolled up in the per-project rollup).

    • What it is: the reusable rule library: one large static partial class split across fifty-three ArchitectureRules.*.cs files, whose methods each assert one architectural invariant across every applicable assembly a map declares. A repo's test classes reduce to a sealed subclass of the matching *TestsBase supplying its own map.
